reason: Arbitrary Python code execution via eval(). User input from request.form['expression'] (line 116) is passed directly to eval() on line 120 with no sanitization: str(eval(expression)). An attacker can execute arbitrary Python code such as __import__('os').system('id').

The result of eval(expression) is concatenated directly into an HTML response string without any output encoding or escaping. Even if eval() only returns data (not code execution), any HTML/JS in the result is rendered in the browser. The response is constructed via string concatenation: '"Result: " + (str(eval(expression))...'.

OS command injection via unsanitized user input. The address parameter from request.form['address'] (line 136) is concatenated directly into a shell command: rp('nslookup ' + address). The rp function references os.popen (imported on line 4). An attacker can inject arbitrary commands using shell metacharacters, e.g. 'example.com; cat /etc/passwd'.

The output of the OS command (nslookup result) is concatenated directly into the HTML response without escaping. The user-supplied address is also reflected in the output. An attacker can inject HTML/JS via the address parameter, which gets rendered in the browser unescaped.

XML External Entity (XXE) injection. The XML parser is created with etree.XMLParser(no_network=False, dtd_validation=True) on line 157, explicitly enabling network access and DTD validation. User-supplied XML from request.form['xml'] is parsed with etree.fromstring() on line 159 without disabling entity resolution (resolve_entities defaults to True in lxml). An attacker can read local files via <!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM 'file:///etc/passwd'> or perform SSRF.

Parsed XML content is rendered directly into the HTML response without escaping on line 169: '(parsed_xml) if parsed_xml else ...'. An attacker can craft XML that, when parsed and rendered, includes HTML/JavaScript that executes in the victim's browser.

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via Jinja2. User input from request.form['name'] (line 189) is embedded into a template string using Python string formatting (%s) on line 204, then the template is rendered with render_template_string() on line 205. Since user input becomes part of the Jinja2 template before rendering, an attacker can inject template expressions like {{config}} or {{''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__()}} to achieve remote code execution.

Reflected XSS in the /sayhi endpoint. User input from request.form['name'] is placed into an HTML string via Python string formatting on line 189: '
Hello %s!

' %(request.form['name']). This string is then embedded into a Jinja2 template via %s substitution (not Jinja2's {{ }} autoescaping), so HTML/JS in the name parameter is rendered unescaped in the browser.

Flask secret key is hardcoded in source code: app.secret_key = 'Harry Potter And The Deathly Hallows'. This key is used to sign session cookies. An attacker who knows this key can forge arbitrary session data (e.g., set logged_in=True) to bypass authentication, or decrypt any signed data.

Passwords are stored in plaintext without hashing. On line 62, the registration handler stores the password directly from the form: User(username=request.form['username'], password=request.form['password']). The User model (line 26) stores passwords as plain strings with no hashing (e.g., bcrypt, scrypt). The `__init__` (line 30) assigns the raw value via `self.password = password`. If the database is compromised, all user passwords are immediately exposed.

Flask debug mode is enabled in production: app.debug = True. This exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger, which allows arbitrary code execution on the server if the debugger PIN is known or brute-forced. It also exposes detailed stack traces, source code, and local variables to any user who triggers an error.

The /evaluate endpoint allows arbitrary code execution but has no authentication check. Unlike the home route which checks session['logged_in'], the evaluate, lookup, xml, and sayhi endpoints are accessible to unauthenticated users, allowing anyone to exploit the code injection vulnerability without logging in.
The /lookup endpoint allows OS command injection but has no authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and execute arbitrary shell commands via the address parameter.
The /xml endpoint allows XXE attacks but has no authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and exploit the XXE vulnerability to read local files or perform SSRF.

The /sayhi endpoint allows SSTI/RCE but has no authentication check. Any unauthenticated user can access this endpoint and exploit the template injection vulnerability to achieve remote code execution.

The login query uses SQLAlchemy ORM's filter_by() method: User.query.filter_by(username=name, password=passw).first(). Although user input (name, passw) flows directly into the query, SQLAlchemy's ORM automatically parameterizes filter_by() arguments, preventing SQL injection. This is NOT vulnerable.

The error template renders {{ error }} using Jinja2's double-curly-brace syntax, which auto-escapes HTML by default. The error object (Flask's 404 error) is rendered safely. This is NOT vulnerable to XSS because Jinja2 autoescaping prevents HTML injection.

The index template renders {{data}} using Jinja2's auto-escaped double-curly-brace syntax. Even if user-controlled data were passed to this template variable, Jinja2 would HTML-escape it before rendering. In practice, the 'data' variable is not even passed from any route handler, so this is doubly safe. This is NOT vulnerable.

The CONFIG dictionary contains a hardcoded 'app_name' string: CONFIG = {'app_name': 'Damn Vulnerable Flask Application'}. While this looks like it could be a configuration with sensitive values, it only contains the application display name. This is NOT a credential or secret — it is a non-sensitive display string used in the HTML title on line 93.

SQL injection via unsanitized 'filter' GraphQL argument directly interpolated into raw SQL using Python string formatting: result.filter(text("title = '%s' or content = '%s'" % (filter, filter))). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via the filter parameter of the pastes query.

OS command injection in ImportPaste mutation. User-controlled host, port, path, and scheme parameters are used to construct a URL that is passed to os.popen via helpers.run_cmd(f'curl --insecure {url}'). In easy mode, strip_dangerous_characters is a no-op. In hard mode, only ';' and '&' are removed, leaving backticks, $(), pipes, and newlines exploitable.

Server-side request forgery in ImportPaste mutation. User controls host, port, path, and scheme parameters which are assembled into a URL and fetched by the server via curl. An attacker can make the server issue requests to internal services (e.g., scheme='http', host='169.254.169.254', path='/latest/meta-data/').

OS command injection via the 'cmd' argument in the systemDiagnostics GraphQL query. In easy mode, security.allowed_cmds() always returns True, so user-supplied cmd is passed directly to os.popen via helpers.run_cmd(cmd). Requires valid admin credentials (hardcoded as admin/changeme), making it an authenticated RCE.

OS command injection via the 'arg' argument in the systemDebug GraphQL query. User-supplied arg is concatenated into a command string: helpers.run_cmd('ps {}'.format(arg)), which executes via os.popen. No authentication or input validation is performed. An attacker can inject arbitrary commands (e.g., arg='aux; id').

Flask SECRET_KEY and JWT_SECRET_KEY are both hardcoded as the string 'dvga'. This allows attackers to forge Flask session cookies and JWT access/refresh tokens, enabling authentication bypass and session hijacking.

JWT signature verification and expiration checking are explicitly disabled: decode(token, options={'verify_signature': False, 'verify_exp': False}). Any attacker can craft a JWT with an arbitrary identity claim (e.g., 'admin') without knowing the secret key, bypassing all authentication on the 'me' query.

Stored XSS via paste title and content rendered unsanitized in JavaScript template literals injected into the DOM via jQuery .append(). User-controlled paste data (title at line 134, content at line 138) from the GraphQL API is interpolated directly into HTML without encoding: $("#public_gallery").append(`...${title}...${content}...`). An attacker can create a paste with malicious HTML/JS content that executes when other users view the pastes page.

Stored XSS via WebSocket subscription handler. Paste data received over the GraphQL subscription WebSocket is interpolated unsanitized into HTML template literals: ${paste.title} (line 66), ${paste.content} (line 70), ${paste.userAgent} (line 73). The resulting HTML is inserted into the DOM via jQuery .prependTo() (lines 77, 79). When a new paste is created with malicious content, it executes in all connected browsers.

Path traversal in file upload via the UploadPaste mutation. The user-supplied filename is concatenated directly to WEB_UPLOADDIR ('pastes/') without any sanitization: f = open(WEB_UPLOADDIR + filename, 'w'). An attacker can use directory traversal sequences (e.g., filename='../../../etc/cron.d/evil') to write arbitrary files on the filesystem.

Detailed stack traces, debug information, and full server file paths are exposed in GraphQL error responses via the /graphiql endpoint. The format_custom_error function includes traceback.format_stack(), traceback.format_exc(), and the full filesystem path of the caller in the 'extensions.exception' field of every error response (except the initial GraphiQL access rejection).

The deleteAllPastes GraphQL query deletes every paste in the database (Paste.query.delete()) without any authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated user can invoke this query to destroy all application data.

Insecure direct object reference in EditPaste mutation. The paste ID is taken directly from user input and used to look up and modify the paste (Paste.query.filter_by(id=id).update(...)) without any ownership or authorization verification. Any user can modify any paste by specifying its ID.

Insecure direct object reference in DeletePaste mutation. The paste ID is taken directly from user input and used to delete the paste (Paste.query.filter_by(id=id).delete()) without any ownership or authorization verification. Any user can delete any paste by specifying its ID.

Hardcoded weak credentials for application users. The admin user is created with password from random_password() which always returns 'changeme' (line 49: weak_passwords = ['changeme']). The operator user is created with plaintext password 'password123'. These credentials are deterministic and publicly known from the source code.

User passwords are stored in plaintext and exposed through the GraphQL API. The resolve_password method returns the actual plaintext password when info.context.json.get('identity') == 'admin'. Since the 'identity' field is set from an unverified JWT token (verify_signature=False in get_identity), any attacker can forge a JWT with identity='admin' and query all user passwords in cleartext.

Denial of service via the systemUpdate GraphQL query. The resolver calls security.simulate_load() which enters a tight loop with time.sleep(0.1) for 200-500 iterations (20-50 seconds of blocking). Combined with GraphQL batch query support (batch=True at line 513), an attacker can send multiple batched systemUpdate queries to exhaust server threads and cause denial of service.

Deep recursion denial of service via circular type references in the GraphQL schema. PasteObject defines an 'owner' field resolving to OwnerObject, and OwnerObject defines a 'pastes' field resolving back to PasteObject. An attacker can craft deeply nested queries like { pastes { owner { pastes { owner { ... } } } } } that cause exponential response growth and server crash. No query depth limiting is enforced at the resolver level in easy mode.

Log injection / log spoofing via user-controlled GraphQL operation names. The Audit.create_audit_entry method records the operation name from GraphQL requests into the audit log without validation. An attacker can assign an innocent operation name (e.g., 'getPastes') to a malicious mutation (e.g., deleteAllPastes), causing audit logs to misrepresent the true nature of the request and evade security monitoring.

Plaintext password storage in User model. The password column is defined as db.Column(db.String(60)) with no hashing mechanism. The create_user classmethod stores the password directly without bcrypt/argon2/scrypt. If the database is compromised, all user passwords are immediately exposed in cleartext, enabling credential stuffing attacks.

Unauthenticated access to all user records via the resolve_users GraphQL resolver. When no id parameter is provided, all User objects are returned including sensitive fields (passwords via resolve_password). No authentication or authorization check is performed. Any anonymous user can enumerate all users and their data.

The /audit HTTP endpoint displays all GraphQL operation audit logs without any authentication check. The audit log contains GraphQL queries which may include sensitive data (tokens, passwords) that bypassed the incomplete clean_query regex sanitization. Any unauthenticated user can view the full audit trail.

The /start_over HTTP endpoint resets the entire application database to its default state by calling helpers.initialize() (which runs python3 setup.py) without any authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated user can trigger complete data destruction by visiting this URL.

The /difficulty/<level> HTTP endpoint allows any unauthenticated user to switch the server from 'hard' mode (with security controls) to 'easy' mode (all security middleware disabled). This disables depth limiting, cost analysis, operation name filtering, deny lists, and introspection blocking without any authentication.

User enumeration via distinct authentication error messages. The check_creds function returns 'Username is invalid' for non-existent usernames vs 'Password Incorrect' for valid usernames with wrong passwords. This allows attackers to enumerate valid usernames by observing the error response difference.

Weak identifier generation. The generate_uuid function truncates UUID4 values to only 6 hex characters (str(uuid.uuid4())[0:6]), providing ~16.7 million possible values instead of the full 2^122 UUID4 space. This makes resource identifiers brute-forceable, enabling IDOR attacks against resources that rely on these short IDs for access control.

GraphiQL access control bypass via client-controlled cookie. The IGQLProtectionMiddleware grants access to the GraphiQL interactive IDE based solely on the client-controlled cookie value: request.cookies.get('env') == 'graphiql:enable'. Since cookies are set by the client, any attacker can bypass this restriction by setting the 'env' cookie to 'graphiql:enable'.

Broken command allow-list due to Python string concatenation bug. The tuple ('echo', 'ps' 'whoami', 'tail') has a missing comma between 'ps' and 'whoami', causing Python implicit string concatenation to produce 'pswhoami' instead of separate 'ps' and 'whoami' entries. This means 'ps' and 'whoami' are not individually in the allow list, making the hard mode command filtering unreliable.

Denylist bypass via batch queries. The processMiddleware only checks queries when info.context.json is a dict (line 95) but does not handle the list case (batch queries). An attacker can send a batch query (JSON array) containing denied queries like systemHealth, completely bypassing the denylist. Other middleware classes (DepthProtection, CostProtection) correctly handle both dict and list cases.

Denylist trivially bypassable via query variations. The on_denylist function only checks for exact matches against two specific normalized query strings ('query{systemHealth}' and '{systemHealth}'). This is trivially bypassed by adding aliases (query{a:systemHealth}), fragments, arguments, comments, or different formatting. The function should use AST-based query analysis rather than string matching.

Incomplete audit log sanitization allows sensitive data leakage. The clean_query function uses fragile regex patterns that only match token:"..." and password:"..." with specific double-quote formatting. Single quotes, alternate field names (passwd, secret, apiKey), whitespace between colon and quote, or other variations bypass sanitization entirely. Sensitive credentials can be stored in plaintext in the audit log table, accessible via the unauthenticated /audit endpoint.

Information disclosure via exception handling in save_file. When a file operation fails (e.g., path traversal attempt hits a permission error), the raw Python exception message is captured via str(e) and returned as the mutation result through UploadPaste. This leaks filesystem paths, permission details, and OS error messages to the client. Distinct from dvga-011 (stack traces in GraphQL error responses) as this leaks through the mutation return value, not through error extensions.

TLS certificate validation disabled in ImportPaste mutation. The curl command at line 211 uses the --insecure flag: helpers.run_cmd(f'curl --insecure {url}'). This disables all SSL/TLS certificate verification, making the server-side request vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. An attacker performing MITM can intercept and modify content fetched by the server, injecting malicious content into imported pastes. Distinct from dvga-002 (command injection) and dvga-003 (SSRF) which cover different vulnerability classes at the same code location.

Missing brute force protection on the Login mutation. The authentication endpoint (lines 225-241) has no rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or progressive delays. Combined with batch query support (batch=True at line 513), an attacker can send thousands of login attempts in a single HTTP request. The hardcoded credentials (admin/changeme per dvga-015) make this especially exploitable, but the missing rate limiting is a distinct vulnerability from the weak credentials themselves.

GraphQL subscription broadcasts all paste creation events to all subscribers without authorization or privacy filtering. The Subscription class (lines 258-262) uses global_event.map(lambda i: i) to forward ALL paste after_insert events, including private pastes (public=False) with their full content, title, and metadata. Any connected WebSocket client — including unauthenticated ones — receives real-time notifications of every paste created, regardless of the paste's visibility setting or the subscriber's identity.

The resolve_search GraphQL resolver returns raw User ORM objects (lines 305-306, 310-311) mixed into the SearchResult union without auth, ownership filtering, or field allowlisting. User objects expose all model columns including the password field via resolve_password, which only gates on a forgeable JWT identity claim per dvga-007. An unauthenticated attacker can dump all users by issuing search with an empty keyword (else branch returns User.query.all()). Distinct from dvga-021 (resolve_users) and dvga-016 (resolve_password field-level sink).

NOT VULNERABLE. The Login mutation passes user-supplied username and password directly to SQLAlchemy's filter_by(): User.query.filter_by(username=username, password=password).first(). While this appears to pass unsanitized input to a database query, SQLAlchemy ORM's filter_by() uses parameterized queries internally, binding values as SQL parameters rather than interpolating them into the query string.

NOT VULNERABLE. The resolve_search method uses Python string formatting to build a LIKE pattern (search = "%{}%".format(keyword)) and passes it to SQLAlchemy's .like() method: Paste.query.filter(Paste.title.like(search)). Despite the string formatting, the value is bound as a SQL parameter by SQLAlchemy's expression API. Compare with the vulnerable resolve_pastes which uses text() with % formatting — here the ORM handles parameterization safely.

NOT VULNERABLE. The audit page renders user-controlled GraphQL operations and queries ({{i.gqloperation}} and {{i.gqlquery}}) in an HTML table. While this data originates from user-submitted GraphQL queries and could contain malicious HTML/JS, Flask's Jinja2 template engine auto-escapes all {{ }} expressions in .html templates by default, converting <, >, &, and quotes to their HTML entity equivalents.

NOT VULNERABLE. The resolve_system_health method calls helpers.run_cmd() which uses os.popen(), but the command string is entirely hardcoded: helpers.run_cmd("uptime | awk -F': ' '{print $2}' | awk -F',' '{print $1}'"). No user input reaches the command string. A scanner may flag the os.popen usage pattern, but without user-controllable input there is no command injection vector.

SQL injection via string formatting in raw query. user_id_form from POST data is interpolated directly into SQL: User.objects.raw('SELECT * FROM %s WHERE user_id=\'%s\' ORDER BY is_admin=\'0\'' % (table_name, user_id_form)). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the user_id POST parameter.

SQL injection via string formatting in raw query. Both ip and col parameters are interpolated directly into SQL: 'SELECT %s FROM %s WHERE ip_address=\'%s\' ORDER BY id DESC' % (col, table_name, ip). The ip parameter comes from request.GET['ip'] in admin_analytics view, and the col parameter is constructed from GET parameter keys.

Remote code execution via insecure deserialization. User-controlled POST parameter 'user' is base64-decoded and passed to pickle.loads(): user = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(encoded_user)). An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to execute arbitrary code on the server.

Remote code execution via eval() on user input. The 'class' GET parameter is passed directly to eval(): model = eval(classname). An attacker can execute arbitrary Python code by passing malicious input as the class parameter.
Remote code execution via eval() on user input. The 'class' GET parameter is passed directly to eval(): model = eval(classname). Same vulnerability as api_index but in a different endpoint (api_id).

OS command injection via os.system() with unsanitized file name. The uploaded file name (orig_file.name) is interpolated into a shell command: os.system('cp %s %s' % (full_file_name, bak_file_path)). An attacker can inject shell commands through a crafted filename.

Arbitrary file read via path traversal. The 'name' GET parameter is concatenated directly to BASE_DIR without sanitization: path = BASE_DIR + r'/' + request.GET.get('name', ''). An attacker can use '../' sequences to read any file on the filesystem.

Open redirect via user-controlled 'path' POST parameter. The path from request.POST['path'] is used directly in HttpResponseRedirect(path) without validation, allowing an attacker to redirect authenticated users to a malicious site.

Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY in settings.py: '+f0x#go-9e-qd(mq0pdn9ma*ls!h+4uy2hcofnep!o0=ow=ewn'. This secret is used for cryptographic signing (sessions, CSRF tokens, etc.). Exposure allows session forgery and CSRF bypass.
Hardcoded encryption key: KEY = b'12345678910111212345678910111212'. This key is used for AES encryption of sensitive data (bank account numbers, SSNs). The key is trivially predictable.
Hardcoded API token salt: ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT = 'S4828341189aefiasd#ASDF'. This salt is used for generating API access tokens. Exposure allows token forgery to access the API as any user.

Hardcoded user credentials in seed data including admin password 'admin1234' (line 16) and other user passwords ('yankeessuck', 'alohaowasp', 'motocross1445', 'citrusblend'). These are default credentials that would be present in any deployment using the seed command.

IDOR leading to sensitive data exposure. The user_id URL parameter is used directly to fetch user data (User.objects.get(id=user_id)) without verifying it matches the authenticated user. Any authenticated user can view another user's work info including SSN and salary by changing the user_id in the URL.

Weak password hashing using MD5. Passwords are hashed with hashlib.md5() which is cryptographically broken for password storage. MD5 is fast and susceptible to rainbow table and brute force attacks. Should use bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2.

Full unencrypted SSN exposed in HTML source. The SSN is rendered as {{ work_info.SSN }} in the HTML. Although JavaScript on lines 47-48 masks it visually with regex replacement, the full SSN is present in the page source and accessible to anyone who views source or disables JavaScript.

Username enumeration via differential error messages. When email is not found, the message is 'Email incorrect!' (line 53). When the email exists but password is wrong, the message is 'Password incorrect!' (line 56). This allows attackers to enumerate valid email addresses.

Username enumeration via password reset. When the email exists, the response is 'An email was sent to reset your password!' (line 20). When it doesn't exist, the response is 'We do not have the email in our system' (line 24). This allows attackers to enumerate valid email addresses.

Missing authorization check on admin dashboard. The @user_is_authenticated decorator only checks if a valid auth_token cookie exists, but does not verify is_admin=True. Any authenticated non-admin user can access admin functionality by navigating to /admin/<id>/dashboard/.

Missing admin authorization on user update endpoint. Any authenticated user can update any user's data including setting is_admin flag via POST to /admin/<id>/update/. The User.objects.filter().update(**data) on line 66 directly applies all POST parameters, allowing privilege escalation.
Missing admin authorization on user deletion. Any authenticated user can delete any user by sending a DELETE request to /admin/<id>/delete/. The decorator only checks authentication, not admin role.

IDOR on message access. The message is fetched by message_id (Message.objects.get(pk=message_id)) without verifying the authenticated user is the message's sender or receiver. Any authenticated user can read or delete any user's messages by changing the message_id in the URL.

Mass assignment vulnerability. All POST parameters are passed directly to User.objects.filter().update(**data) without filtering allowed fields. An attacker can set arbitrary model fields including is_admin, auth_token, user_id, etc.

Django DEBUG mode is enabled (DEBUG = True). In production, this exposes detailed stack traces, settings, SQL queries, and local variables to any user who triggers an error, leaking sensitive information about the application internals.
ALLOWED_HOSTS set to ['*'] which accepts requests with any Host header. This can enable host header injection attacks, cache poisoning, and password reset poisoning.

Predictable password reset token using MD5. Token is generated as user_id + '-' + MD5(email). Since user_id and email are often known or guessable, an attacker can forge valid password reset tokens and take over any account without needing access to the reset email.

No authentication required for password reset endpoint. The reset_password_handler and reset_password functions have no authentication decorator. Combined with the predictable token (djangoat-025) and pickle deserialization (djangoat-003), this enables unauthenticated account takeover and RCE.

Stored XSS via mark_safe() on user-controlled data. The safe_name() method calls mark_safe(self.first_name) which marks the user's first name as safe HTML, bypassing Django's auto-escaping. If a user registers with a first_name containing JavaScript (e.g., <script>alert(1)</script>), it will be rendered unescaped wherever safe_name is used.

Broken API authentication via weak regex-based token validation. The comment on line 41 explicitly states 'This is purposely vulnerable'. The regex '(.*?)-(.*)' is overly permissive - group(1) captures everything before the first dash. Combined with the hardcoded ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT, an attacker who knows the salt can forge tokens for any user.

Authentication cookie set without Secure or HttpOnly flags. The auth_token cookie is set via response.set_cookie('auth_token', user.auth_token) without secure=True or httponly=True parameters. This makes the token accessible to JavaScript (enabling theft via XSS) and transmittable over unencrypted HTTP.

Path traversal in file upload. The uploaded file name (uploaded_file.name) is used directly in os.path.join(data_path, uploaded_file.name) without sanitization. An attacker can upload files to arbitrary locations by using '../' in the filename.

IDOR on pay record deletion. Pay.objects.get(id=pay_id).delete() deletes any pay record by ID without verifying the authenticated user owns that record. Any authenticated user can delete another user's direct deposit information.

Weak auth token generation using MD5 with limited randomness. Token is generated as MD5(email + random(1,1000000)). The random space is only 1 million values, and MD5 is fast, making brute-force feasible. An attacker who knows a user's email can generate all possible tokens quickly.

DOM-based XSS via document.write() on signup page. The template reads the URL hash fragment (location.hash), decodes it with decodeURIComponent(), and passes it directly to document.write() without sanitization. An attacker can craft a URL like /signup#lang=<script>alert(document.cookie)</script> to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser, stealing the auth_token cookie. This is a distinct client-side XSS not covered by the existing stored XSS finding (djangoat-027 covers mark_safe in user.py).

Broken CSRF protection due to template tag typo. The CSRF token tag is malformed: '{ % crsf_token % }' instead of '{% csrf_token %}'. The extra spaces inside braces and the typo 'crsf' (instead of 'csrf') mean the token is never rendered, leaving the admin user update/delete form without CSRF protection. An attacker can craft a page that auto-submits requests to modify or delete users when an authenticated admin visits it.

XSS via unquoted HTML attribute values in admin modal template. The template renders user fields in HTML attributes without quotes (e.g., value={{user.email}}). Even with Django's autoescaping, unquoted attribute values allow attribute injection — an attacker who controls the email field can inject additional HTML attributes like 'test onfocus=alert(1) autofocus' to execute JavaScript in the admin's browser context.

XSS via Django template variable rendered inside JavaScript string literal. The performance template renders review.date_for_chart inside a JS string using Django template tags without the |escapejs filter. Django's auto-escaping only escapes HTML entities (<, >, &, etc.) but not JavaScript string delimiters (single quotes, backslashes). If an attacker controls performance review data, they can inject JavaScript that executes in other users' browsers when viewing performance pages.

Use of deprecated PyCrypto library with AES-CBC mode for encrypting sensitive data (SSNs, bank account numbers). PyCrypto is unmaintained and has known vulnerabilities (e.g., heap buffer overflow CVE-2013-7459). AES-CBC without message authentication (no HMAC/AEAD) is vulnerable to padding oracle and bit-flipping attacks. This is distinct from djangoat-010 which covers the hardcoded encryption key.

Static IV reuse with AES-CBC mode. The get_iv() method retrieves a static IV from the KeyManagement model for each user, reusing it for every encryption operation. In AES-CBC, reusing the same key+IV combination for different plaintexts leaks information about plaintext relationships and undermines semantic security. This is distinct from the hardcoded key issue (djangoat-010).

Padding oracle vulnerability via custom PKCS7 padding removal without authenticated encryption. The unpad method performs s[:-ord(s[len(s)-1:])] without integrity verification. Combined with AES-CBC mode, this creates a classic padding oracle where an attacker can manipulate ciphertext and observe differential error behavior to decrypt sensitive data (SSNs, bank account numbers) byte-by-byte without the key.

Session fixation via static auth_token that is never regenerated upon login. The login handler authenticates the user and sets the auth_token cookie, but the token is the same static value stored in the database — never rotated on authentication. If an attacker can preset or predict a user's token (feasible given djangoat-032's weak generation), they retain access post-authentication. This is distinct from djangoat-029 (missing cookie flags) and djangoat-032 (weak token entropy).

Password reset token has no expiration. The is_valid_token function only checks that the MD5 hash matches the user's email — there is no timestamp or expiration check. Tokens remain valid indefinitely. A token intercepted via email logs, referrer headers, or network interception can be used at any time in the future for account takeover. This is distinct from djangoat-025 which covers token predictability.

Hardcoded database credentials in Docker settings: username 'root' with password 'password'. These are committed to source control and use the database superuser account with a trivially guessable password. This is a separate settings file (docker_settings.py) from the secrets in pygoat/settings.py already covered by djangoat-009/010/011, and covers database credentials specifically.

Message spoofing via unvalidated creator_id in POST data. The user_messages POST handler takes creator_id from request.POST['creator_id'] without verifying it matches the authenticated user. An attacker can send messages impersonating any user by setting creator_id to another user's ID. This is distinct from djangoat-021 which covers IDOR on message READ/DELETE access — this finding is about message CREATION with forged sender identity.

No authentication on mobile API endpoints. The api_index mobile endpoint has no authentication or authorization checks — any unauthenticated user can access it. Even without the eval() vulnerability (djangoat-004), if the class parameter is 'User', all user records including PII are returned without authentication. This is a distinct vulnerability (missing authentication) from the code injection via eval() already in ground truth.

NOT VULNERABLE. The update dict passed to User.objects.filter(pk=user.pk).update(**update) is populated only by User.validate_update_form (app/models/User/user.py:173-195), which writes exactly four hard-coded keys: password, email, first_name and last_name. The keys are string literals, not derived from the submitted form keys, so no privileged field such as is_admin can be injected. This is an explicit allowlist.

Hardcoded plaintext credentials for multiple user accounts (including admin) exposed in a public-facing template. The not_logged_in.html template serves these credentials to unauthenticated visitors in the HTML source. This is distinct from djangoat-012 (seed.py credentials requiring file system access) — these credentials are served directly over HTTP to any visitor without authentication, making them immediately exploitable for account takeover including the admin account.

Mass data exposure via admin API endpoint that serializes ALL User objects with ALL fields using serializers.serialize('json', User.objects.all()). No field-level filtering restricts which attributes are returned, exposing passwords/hashes, auth tokens, PII, and internal state for every user. Combined with the broken token authentication (djangoat-028), any attacker who forges an admin token gets access to all user data. This is distinct from djangoat-028 which covers the broken auth mechanism — this finding covers the data over-exposure at the endpoint itself.

DOM-based XSS via jQuery .html() method in decryptDirectDeposit function. The server response from the decrypt endpoint is inserted directly into the DOM using .html() without sanitization. If the decrypted bank account data contains user-controlled content (e.g., account holder name or memo), an attacker could store a JavaScript payload that executes when the data is decrypted and rendered. Additionally, the jQuery selector uses string concatenation with user input: $('.accNum:contains(\'' + input + '\')'), enabling selector injection.

Reflected XSS via user_id_form from POST data rendered in HttpResponse without HTML escaping. At line 80, HttpResponse('User ' + str(user_id_form) + ' NOT FOUND') reflects the user-supplied POST parameter directly in the response body. An attacker can inject HTML/JavaScript via the user_id POST field. This is distinct from djangoat-001 which covers SQL injection on the same input — this finding covers the separate XSS vulnerability when the SQL query returns no results.

NOT VULNERABLE. Every route binding user_view constrains the parameter to digits: url(r'^(?P<user_id>[0-9]+)$', ...) in app/views/users/urls.py:15. user_id therefore cannot carry angle brackets or quotes into the HttpResponse at views.py:101, and request.method is restricted to four fixed tokens by @require_http_methods.

Authentication cookie set without Secure or HttpOnly flags in the signup auto-login flow. After creating and authenticating a new user, the index view sets the session credential via response.set_cookie('auth_token', auth.auth_token) with no secure=True or httponly=True parameters. This makes the auth_token readable by JavaScript (enabling theft via the application's XSS sinks) and transmittable over unencrypted HTTP. This is a distinct sink from djangoat-029, which covers the same weakness in the login flow (app/views/sessions/views.py); the scorer matches on file+CWE+line so the two locations do not overlap.

NOT VULNERABLE as cleartext storage. A pre_save receiver on User (app/signals.py:8-13) calls instance.hash_password() unconditionally, outside the 'if instance.pk is None' guard, and app/models/__init__.py:13 imports app.signals. User.objects.create() therefore hashes the password before the row is written. The hash is MD5, which is a weak-hash weakness (CWE-328) recorded separately, not cleartext storage.

NOT VULNERABLE. The parse_field() method validates the field parameter against an allowlist of valid_fields = ['ip_address', 'referrer', 'user_agent']. If the field is not in the list, it returns '1'. This prevents SQL injection through field name manipulation.

NOT VULNERABLE. The selected_id is cast to int() before being passed to User.objects.get(user_id=int(selected_id)). The Django ORM parameterizes the query. The int() cast prevents any SQL injection via the URL parameter.
NOT VULNERABLE. User.objects.filter(email=request.POST.get('email', '')) uses Django's ORM with keyword argument filtering, which parameterizes the query. User input is not interpolated into raw SQL.

NOT VULNERABLE. {{ message.message }} uses Django's default auto-escaping which escapes <, >, &, ', and " characters. The message content is properly escaped before rendering in the template. The |safe filter is not used.

PARTIALLY MITIGATED but still vulnerable (see djangoat-030). The data_path uses os.path.join(settings.MEDIA_ROOT, 'data') which is a fixed base path, but the uploaded_file.name on line 33 is not sanitized. Note: os.path.join with an absolute second argument would replace the first, but Django's UploadedFile.name is typically relative. The real risk is in the filename containing traversal sequences. Documenting as FP for the data_path construction itself.

NOT a real credential exposure. The reviewer_data tuple contains test/fixture data used for build_benefits_data() including 'auth_token' as a literal string value. This is test data internal to the application's data seeding, not a real authentication credential that grants access.

SQL injection via string concatenation in SQLinjection.run(). The 'id' parameter from request is concatenated directly into SQL: cursor.execute("SELECT ... WHERE id=" + id). No parameterization or input validation.

SQL injection in AuthBypass.run() via the password parameter. The password is concatenated directly into the login query: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username='" + username + "' AND password='" + password + "'"). While username is sanitized with re.sub(r"[^\w]", '', ...), the password parameter has no sanitization, enabling authentication bypass via SQLi payloads like ' OR '1'='1.

Reflected XSS in XSSReflected.run(). The 'msg' parameter from the request is returned directly as HTML content without any escaping or sanitization: content = content[0]. Injecting <script>alert(1)</script> as the msg parameter executes arbitrary JavaScript.

Stored XSS in XSSStored.run(). Comments retrieved from the database are rendered into HTML table cells without escaping: columns += "{}".format(column). Although comments are stored via parameterized INSERT (preventing SQLi), no output encoding is applied when rendering, so stored XSS payloads execute for every visitor.

Open redirect in UnvalidatedRedirect.run(). The 'path' parameter is injected directly into a JavaScript window.location.replace() call via Python string formatting: window.location.replace('{path}'). An attacker can redirect users to arbitrary URLs. Additionally, since the value is injected into a <script> context, a payload like ');alert(1);// achieves XSS.

OS command injection in CommandInjection.run(). The 'domain' parameter is concatenated with the command name and passed to subprocess.check_output() with shell=True: subprocess.check_output(' '.join([command, domain]), shell=True, ...). Payloads like 'google.com;whoami' execute arbitrary commands. Requires risk level 3.

Insecure deserialization via pickle in UnsafeDeserialization.run(). User-supplied base64-encoded data is decoded and passed directly to pickle.loads(): pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(object)). A crafted pickle payload with __reduce__ achieves arbitrary code execution. Requires risk level 3.

Path traversal in PathTraversal.run(). The 'path' parameter is passed to open() after os.path.abspath() which does NOT prevent traversal: file = open(os.path.abspath(path), 'rb'). A payload like '../../etc/passwd' reads arbitrary files. The only check is whether '://' is in the path (which routes to SSRF instead).

SSRF in PathTraversal.run(). When the 'path' parameter contains '://', it is passed directly to urllib.request.urlopen(path), allowing the attacker to make requests to arbitrary URLs including internal services (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/ for cloud metadata).

Session fixation in SessionFixation.run(). The 'session' parameter from the request is directly set as the SESSIONID cookie: cookie['SESSIONID'] = session. An attacker can send a victim a link with a pre-set session ID, then hijack the session after the victim authenticates.

Execution After Redirect (EAR) in ExecutionAfterRedirect.run(). The /admin page renders sensitive admin content (Manage Users, Update Database Settings links) before checking authentication. The redirect to /login is done via client-side JavaScript (window.location), which can be blocked by the browser or intercepted, allowing unauthenticated users to see admin page content.

Cross-Site Request Forgery in XSRequestForgery.run(). The settings form at /settings uses GET method with no CSRF token. An attacker can craft a link or image tag that changes a user's email address: /settings?email=attacker@evil.com. The state-changing operation (email update) has no anti-CSRF protection.

Clickjacking vulnerability in Clickjacking.run(). The /danger endpoint performs account deletion via GET request with no CSRF token and no X-Frame-Options header. The page can be embedded in an iframe on a malicious site, tricking users into clicking the delete button. The destructive action (DELETE FROM users) is triggered by a simple GET with ?delete=1.

Critical command injection via custom HTTP method BDR in do_BDR(). The URL path (self.path[1:]) is passed directly to subprocess.check_output() with shell=True: subprocess.check_output(self.path[1:], shell=True, ...). Any command can be executed by sending a BDR HTTP request with the command as the URL path. Requires risk level 3.

DOM-based XSS in custom.js. The URL fragment (document.location.hash) is decoded and injected directly into the page via document.write() without sanitization: document.write('' + decodeURIComponent(document.location.hash.substring(index + 5)) + ''). A URL like /#lang= executes arbitrary JavaScript. This affects every page that includes custom.js.

Hardcoded backdoor credentials in AuthBypass.run(). The code contains a hardcoded check: if username == 'dsvpwa' and password == 'dsvpwa', which bypasses the database authentication entirely. This is a backdoor account that grants access regardless of database contents.

Plaintext credentials stored in users.xml data file. All user passwords are stored in cleartext including admin (Y3RFgwZP$v6v#D), guest (guest), loella (babygirl), and weitzel (123456). This file is used to seed the database at startup.

Information disclosure in SQLinjection.run(). SQLite OperationalError exceptions are caught and returned directly to the user: return e. This reveals database schema information, table names, and query structure to attackers, aiding further SQL injection exploitation.

Information disclosure in AuthBypass.run(). SQLite OperationalError exceptions from the login query are caught and returned to the user: return content.format(type=type, message=e). This reveals database error details including table/column names and query structure.

Insecure SSL/TLS configuration in main(). Three dangerous SSL options are explicitly enabled: (1) SSLv3 re-enabled via ctx.options &= ~ssl.OP_NO_SSLv3 (vulnerable to POODLE), (2) TLS compression re-enabled via &= ~ssl.OP_NO_COMPRESSION (vulnerable to CRIME), (3) cipher server preference disabled via &= ~ssl.OP_CIPHER_SERVER_PREFERENCE (allows client to choose weak ciphers).

Session cookies set without HttpOnly or Secure flags. At line 234, cookies are output via morsel.OutputString() without setting httponly or secure attributes. Only 'path' is set to '/'. This allows JavaScript to access session cookies (enabling session theft via XSS) and cookies to be transmitted over unencrypted connections.

XSS protection explicitly disabled via response header. X-XSS-Protection is set to '0', disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter. While modern browsers have deprecated this header, disabling it removes a defense-in-depth layer in older browsers.

Weak Content-Security-Policy header. CSP is set to "default-src * 'unsafe-inline'" which allows loading resources from any origin and inline script execution, effectively providing no protection against XSS attacks. This is intentionally weak to enable the XSS attack vectors.

Login form uses GET method: <form id="login" method="GET" action="/login">. Credentials (username and password) are transmitted as URL query parameters, which are logged in browser history, server access logs, proxy logs, and Referer headers. Passwords should never be sent via GET.

Passwords stored in plaintext in the database. User passwords from users.xml are inserted directly into SQLite without hashing: INSERT INTO users(..., password, ...) VALUES(NULL, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?). The password column in the users table (line 33) stores raw plaintext passwords, making all credentials recoverable if the database is compromised.

Weak session token generation using Python's random module instead of cryptographically secure alternatives. Session tokens are generated with random.sample(string.ascii_letters + string.digits, 20), which uses the Mersenne Twister PRNG. This is predictable and not suitable for security-sensitive operations. Should use secrets.token_urlsafe() or os.urandom().

Open redirect in SessionFixation.run(). The 'path' parameter is injected into a JavaScript window.location assignment without validation: window.location = '{path}'. This is a secondary vulnerability in the session fixation handler - in addition to fixing the session, the redirect destination is also attacker-controlled.

Path traversal in StaticHandler.find(). The URL path is used directly in file open calls: open('./{}'.format(path), 'rb') and open('./{}'.format(path), 'r'). No path sanitization or directory restriction is applied. Requests like /static/../../etc/passwd (with an appropriate extension to bypass route matching) read arbitrary files from the filesystem.

The AuthBypass.run() handler at /login has no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism, allowing unlimited brute-force login attempts. The login form also uses GET method, exposing credentials in URLs and server logs. No existing ground truth entry covers the absence of brute-force protection on this endpoint — dsvpwa-002 covers SQL injection in the same handler, and dsvpwa-024 covers GET-method credential exposure in the template, but neither addresses the missing rate limiting.

The 'cookie' attribute is defined as a class variable on VulnHTTPRequestHandler (line 141), meaning it is shared across all request handler instances. In Python's http.server framework, this causes one user's session cookie state to leak to another concurrent user's request, enabling session confusion/hijacking. This is distinct from dsvpwa-010 (session fixation via user-controlled parameter), dsvpwa-021 (missing HttpOnly flag), and dsvpwa-026 (weak PRNG for token generation).

The global exception handler in do_GET at handlers.py lines 216-218 sends raw exception messages to the client via 'content = str(ex)'. This can expose internal implementation details including file paths, module names, and exception types from any unhandled exception during request processing. This is a separate sink from the CWE-209 entries in ground truth (dsvpwa-018 at attacks.py:40-41 and dsvpwa-019 at attacks.py:290-291), which cover specific SQLite error disclosure in individual attack handlers.

The guestbook comment form at templates/guestbook.html:27 uses method='GET' with no anti-CSRF token, allowing an attacker to trick a user into submitting arbitrary comments via a crafted link (e.g., /guestbook?comment=malicious). This is a distinct CSRF from dsvpwa-012 which covers the /settings endpoint (email change) and dsvpwa-013 which covers /danger (account deletion). Lower impact than those entries but a genuine, independently exploitable CSRF on a state-changing operation.

NOT VULNERABLE. XSSStored.run() uses parameterized query for INSERT: cursor.execute('INSERT INTO comments VALUES(NULL, ?, ?)', [comment, time.ctime()]). The ? placeholders properly bind the user-supplied comment value, preventing SQL injection. The stored XSS vulnerability exists in the output rendering (line 97), not in the database insertion.

NOT VULNERABLE. SessionHijacking.run() uses parameterized query: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE session = ?", [session]). The session value from the cookie is bound via placeholder, preventing SQL injection.

NOT VULNERABLE. XSRequestForgery.run() uses parameterized query for SELECT: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE session = ?", [session]). The session cookie value is properly bound via placeholder.

NOT VULNERABLE. XSRequestForgery.run() uses parameterized query for UPDATE: cursor.execute("UPDATE users SET email = ? WHERE id = ?", (email, user[0])). Both the email value and user ID are bound via placeholders.
NOT VULNERABLE. Clickjacking.run() uses parameterized query for SELECT: cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE session = ?", [session]). The session cookie value is properly bound.

NOT VULNERABLE (for the username parameter). AuthBypass.run() sanitizes the username with re.sub(r"[^\w]", '', params.get('username')[0]), stripping all non-word characters. This prevents SQL injection through the username parameter. Note: the password parameter on line 289 IS vulnerable to SQL injection.
SQL injection via id parameter directly concatenated into SELECT query without sanitization
Reflected XSS via v parameter injected into HTML response via re.sub without escaping
Arbitrary code execution via pickle.loads on user-controlled object parameter
Path traversal via path parameter passed to open() with os.path.abspath but no path restriction
SSRF via path parameter passed to urllib.request.urlopen when URL scheme is detected
OS command injection via domain parameter concatenated into nslookup command with shell=True
XXE via xml parameter parsed by lxml with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False
XPath injection via name parameter directly interpolated into XPath query string
Memory-based DoS via size parameter controlling O(n^2) string allocation with no upper bound
SQL injection via comment parameter directly interpolated into INSERT statement with string formatting
Stored XSS via comments rendered from database into HTML without any output encoding
Remote code execution via include parameter: fetches arbitrary local/remote file and passes it to exec()
Open redirect via redir parameter injected into meta refresh URL without validation
Reflected XSS via unsanitized JSONP callback parameter allowing arbitrary JavaScript execution
SQL injection via password parameter in login query concatenated without sanitization, enabling authentication bypass
HTTP header injection via charset parameter injected into Content-Type header without CRLF filtering
Plaintext hardcoded passwords in USERS_XML constant including admin password '7en8aiDoh!'
Full stack trace returned to client via traceback.format_exc() on any unhandled exception
DOM-based XSS via document.write with decodeURIComponent of location.hash fragment in inline JavaScript
Cross-Site Request Forgery on comment submission endpoint — state-changing operation via GET request with no CSRF token, allowing attackers to forge requests that insert comments on behalf of victims
Login endpoint at /login has no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism, allowing unlimited brute-force credential guessing attempts
User passwords from USERS_XML are inserted into SQLite database in plaintext without any hashing via cursor.executemany — extractable via SQL injection

Session IDs generated using random.sample() with Python's Mersenne Twister PRNG which is not cryptographically secure — PRNG state is predictable after observing enough outputs, enabling session ID prediction and session hijacking

Parameter parsing concatenates multiple values for the same parameter name with commas via re.findall and join, enabling HTTP Parameter Pollution to bypass SQL injection sanitization on the login endpoint by splitting payloads across multiple password parameters
SESSIONID cookie set via meta http-equiv tag without HttpOnly or Secure flags — accessible to JavaScript (enabling theft via XSS) and transmittable over unencrypted connections

NOT VULNERABLE by current guidance. X-XSS-Protection: 0 disables the legacy browser XSS auditor, which is deprecated and removed from current browsers and could itself be abused. Setting the header to 0 is the value the OWASP Secure Headers Project recommends, so this is the intended configuration rather than a misconfiguration.

The /users.json endpoint returns all usernames and surnames from USERS_XML to any unauthenticated caller without any access control or authentication check. This is a distinct vulnerability from the JSONP callback XSS (dsvw-014) — fixing the XSS by sanitizing the callback does not address the unauthenticated data exposure, and vice versa. Any anonymous HTTP client can enumerate every user in the system by simply requesting /users.json.
Username parameter in login query is sanitized with re.sub(r'[^\w]', '', ...) stripping all non-word characters before concatenation, preventing SQL injection through the username field
cursor.executemany uses parameterized query with ? placeholders — not vulnerable despite dynamic data insertion
NAME variable is passed through html.escape() before insertion into HTML title via %s formatting — properly sanitized
CREATE TABLE statement is a static string literal with no user input — not vulnerable despite cursor.execute usage

SQL injection via f-string interpolation in login query: query = f"SELECT * FROM user WHERE username = '{username}'". The username parameter from user input is directly interpolated into the SQL string, allowing authentication bypass (e.g., ' OR '1'='1' --) and data exfiltration.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation in registration INSERT query: insert_query = f"INSERT INTO user (username, password_hash, balance) VALUES ('{username}', '{password_hash}', 0000.00)". Both username and password_hash are interpolated directly, allowing SQL injection through the username field.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation in transaction search: query = f"SELECT * FROM \"transaction\" WHERE ... AND description LIKE '%{search_term}%'". The search_term from request.args is directly interpolated, allowing UNION-based extraction of data from other tables.

SQL injection via user-controlled user_id parameter: user_id = request.args.get('user_id', current_user.id) is directly interpolated into f-string SQL query on line 49. An attacker can provide a crafted user_id parameter to inject SQL. Also constitutes an IDOR since any user_id can be specified.
Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'supersecret'. This key is used by Flask for session signing. A known secret allows session forgery.
Hardcoded JWT signing secret: jwt.encode(..., 'secret', algorithm='HS256'). The trivially guessable secret 'secret' allows any attacker to forge valid JWT tokens and impersonate any user.
Hardcoded JWT verification secret: jwt.decode(token, 'secret', algorithms=['HS256']). Same trivial secret 'secret' used for token verification, confirming token forgery is possible.

Weak password hashing using MD5: hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest(). MD5 is cryptographically broken, has no salt, and is computationally fast, making brute-force and rainbow table attacks trivial.
Weak password hashing using MD5 during registration: password_hash = hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest(). Same weak MD5 hashing without salt as in the User model.

IDOR in password update: the user_id is taken from the request body (data.get('user_id')) instead of from the authenticated token (current_user.id). Any authenticated user can change any other user's password by supplying a different user_id. No old password verification is required either.

IDOR in transaction listing: user_id = request.args.get('user_id', current_user.id) allows any authenticated user to view another user's transactions by passing a different user_id parameter. No ownership validation is performed.

Insecure YAML deserialization: yaml.load(profile_yaml, Loader=yaml.Loader) uses the unsafe yaml.Loader which allows arbitrary Python object instantiation and code execution. An attacker can craft a YAML payload with !!python/object/apply to achieve RCE.

Flask debug mode enabled in production: app.run(host='0.0.0.0', debug=True, port=5000). Debug mode exposes the Werkzeug debugger which can allow arbitrary code execution if the debugger PIN is guessed or leaked, and exposes detailed stack traces.

Insecure CORS configuration: the server reflects any Origin header back in Access-Control-Allow-Origin with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. This allows any malicious website to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the API, enabling CSRF-like attacks and data theft.

Sensitive PII (Social Security Numbers) stored in plaintext in user profile data: 'ssn': '123-45-6789'. SSNs are stored as plain JSON in the profile column and exposed via the /api/me endpoint which returns the full profile including SSN.

The /api/me endpoint returns the full user profile including sensitive PII (SSN, DOB, full address) via current_user.get_profile(). The profile JSON is returned in its entirety without filtering sensitive fields.

No server-side session invalidation on logout: the logout endpoint returns a success message but the JWT token remains valid. There is no token blacklist or revocation mechanism, so a stolen token continues to work after the user logs out.

Missing negative amount validation in transfer: amount = Decimal(str(data.get('amount', 0))) accepts negative values. A negative transfer amount would reverse the money flow, effectively stealing money from the recipient. No minimum/maximum amount checks exist.

Race condition (TOCTOU) in transfer: the balance check on line 30 (current_user.balance < amount) and balance deduction on line 33 are not atomic. Concurrent requests can pass the balance check simultaneously, allowing double-spending beyond the actual balance.
Hardcoded secret key in docker-compose environment: SECRET_KEY=supersecret. The same weak, guessable secret is hardcoded in the deployment configuration.

Missing old password verification in password update: the endpoint allows changing the password without verifying the current password. Combined with the IDOR (dvblab-010), this means any authenticated user can change any user's password without knowing the old one.

The registration endpoint at /api/register has no rate limiting, allowing unlimited account creation. The endpoint also enables username enumeration through the 'Username already exists' error response at line 19. An attacker can brute-force usernames or flood the system with accounts. Combined with the weak MD5 password hashing (dvblab-008/009), mass-created accounts with known passwords could be used for further attacks.

Safe ORM query: User.query.filter_by(username=username).first() uses SQLAlchemy's ORM parameterized query API. Despite accepting user input, the filter_by method properly parameterizes the query, preventing SQL injection.

Properly authorized single transaction endpoint: get_transaction checks ownership on line 72 (transaction.sender_id != current_user.id and transaction.receiver_id != current_user.id) and returns 403 if the user is not the sender or receiver. This is NOT an IDOR despite accepting a user-controlled transaction_id.

Safe ORM query: Transaction.query.get(transaction_id) uses SQLAlchemy's ORM primary key lookup which is parameterized. The transaction_id comes from a URL parameter typed as int, and the ORM handles parameterization. Not vulnerable to SQL injection.

Safe JSON deserialization: json.loads(self.profile) uses Python's standard json module which only deserializes to basic Python types (dicts, lists, strings, numbers). Unlike yaml.load or pickle, json.loads cannot instantiate arbitrary objects and is safe from deserialization attacks.

SQL injection via Python string formatting. The 'name' parameter from user input is interpolated directly into the SQL query using Python's % operator: "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name}. The resulting string is then passed to cur.execute(q) without parameterization. An attacker can submit a name like "Robert'); DROP TABLE students CASCADE; --" to execute arbitrary SQL. Documented in the project README.

Stored XSS via review text. The {{ review.review_text }} expression renders user-submitted review text without HTML escaping (autoescape is disabled globally in app.py). Any user can submit a review containing arbitrary HTML/JavaScript (e.g. <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>) via POST to /courses/{id}/review without authentication. The payload is stored in the database and rendered to every user who views the course page. Documented in the project README.

Stored XSS via student names. The {{ name }} expression in the students listing renders student names without HTML escaping. Student names are user-supplied via POST to /students/ (which has no backend authorization check). An attacker can create a student with a name containing JavaScript (e.g. <script>alert(1)</script>) and the payload will execute for every user viewing the students list page.

Stored XSS via course title and description. Lines 14-15 render {{ course.title }} and {{ course.description }} without HTML escaping. Course data is user-supplied via POST to /courses/ (backend has no admin authorization check despite the template gating the form). An attacker can create a course with XSS payloads in the title or description fields.

Stored XSS via course title and description in the courses listing page. Lines 17-18 render {{ course.title }} and {{ course.description }} without HTML escaping. Same root data as dvpwa-004 but a different rendering location affecting the courses index page.

Stored XSS via course title and description on the individual student page. Lines 19-20 render {{ course.title }} and {{ course.description }} without HTML escaping in the marks/results section. Same root data as dvpwa-004 but rendered on the student detail page.

Jinja2 template engine configured with autoescape=False. This disables automatic HTML escaping for all template variables, making every unescaped template expression a potential XSS sink. This is the root cause of all stored XSS vulnerabilities (dvpwa-002 through dvpwa-006). The secure default should be autoescape=True.

Passwords are hashed using unsalted MD5: md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest(). MD5 is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password storage. The lack of salt means identical passwords produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow table attacks and statistical analysis. Passwords should use bcrypt, argon2, or PBKDF2. Documented in the project README.

CSRF protection is disabled. The csrf_middleware is commented out on line 27 (# csrf_middleware,) in the Application middlewares list. Although CSRF tokens are generated in templates, the middleware that validates them on POST requests is never active. This allows cross-site request forgery attacks against all state-changing endpoints. Documented as a vulnerability category in the project README.

Session cookie created with httponly=False. The RedisStorage is configured with httponly=False, meaning the AIOHTTP_SESSION cookie is accessible to JavaScript via document.cookie. Combined with the stored XSS vulnerabilities, this enables session hijacking. The cookie should have httponly=True to prevent JavaScript access.

The 500 error page renders {{ error.__dict__ }} in a <pre> tag, exposing the full internal error object dictionary to the client. This can leak stack traces, internal file paths, database query details, configuration values, and other sensitive server-side information to attackers.

Missing server-side authorization on student creation. The students view handles POST requests to create students without checking if the user is authenticated. The template (students.jinja2) only shows the form to authenticated users, but the backend performs no auth check. Any unauthenticated user can POST directly to /students/ to create student records.

Missing server-side authorization on course creation. The courses view handles POST requests to create courses without checking if the user is authenticated or is an admin. The template (courses.jinja2) only shows the form to admin users, but the backend performs no auth or admin check. Any unauthenticated user can POST directly to /courses/ to create course records.

Session fixation vulnerability. On successful login, the session ID is not rotated — the existing session simply has 'user_id' set (session['user_id'] = user.id) without creating a new session. An attacker who knows a victim's pre-authentication session ID (e.g. via the AIOHTTP_SESSION cookie) can hijack the authenticated session after the victim logs in. Documented in the project README.

Application runs with debug=True in the Application constructor. Debug mode can expose verbose error messages, stack traces, and internal application state to end users, aiding attackers in reconnaissance.

Redis config schema and connection code have no password support. The CONFIG_SCHEMA does not include a password field and aioredis.create_pool() in sqli/services/redis.py does not pass one. This architecturally prevents Redis authentication even if desired, leaving session data accessible to anyone with network access to the Redis instance.

No rate limiting on the login endpoint. The index view handles authentication via POST with no throttling, lockout, or delay mechanism. Combined with weak MD5 password hashing (dvpwa-008), this enables practical online brute-force and credential stuffing attacks.

No rate limiting on non-authentication form submission endpoints. The POST handlers for students, courses, and reviews in views.py have no throttling or abuse prevention. While less critical than the login endpoint (dvpwa-017), this enables automated data creation, resource exhaustion, and potential abuse of the application.

NOT VULNERABLE. auth_user_processor (sqli/utils/jinja2.py:19-21) does place the full User tuple in the template context, but no template renders pwd_hash or the object as a whole. The templates reference only auth_user.first_name, .middle_name, .last_name and .is_admin, so the hash never reaches a response.

Database DSN constructed via string formatting with plaintext password. The _init_pg function builds a DSN string by interpolating config values including the password: 'password={password}'.format(**conf). However, the DSN is a local variable used only during startup, is not logged by any code path, and is not exposed via error pages (startup errors occur before the HTTP server runs). Standard Python tracebacks show source lines, not interpolated variable values. The password already exists in cleartext in the config YAML and app['config']['db'] dict, making the DSN no more risky. Using keyword arguments to aiopg.create_pool() would be marginally better defensive practice.

No TLS/SSL configuration for PostgreSQL connection. The DSN does not include sslmode and no ssl argument is passed to aiopg.create_pool(). However, the deployment context significantly mitigates this: Docker Compose places postgres, redis, and the app on the same internal bridge network — traffic never leaves the host. No production config exists (only config/dev.yaml), the application is open-source and educational, and the database credentials are already postgres:postgres. Per severity guidance for insecure default settings in open-source local development features: Low.

The application bundles jQuery v3.2.1, which has documented CVEs including prototype pollution (CVE-2019-11358) and XSS (CVE-2020-11022, CVE-2020-11023). Exploiting the XSS CVEs requires passing attacker-controlled strings to vulnerable jQuery DOM manipulation methods (.html(), .append(), etc.). The existing templates do not show obvious such patterns, and the dominant XSS risk is server-side via autoescape=False (dvpwa-002 through dvpwa-007). However, having a known-CVE library bundled in the application is a genuine low-severity hardening concern.

course.title is rendered without escaping ({{ course.title }}) while autoescape=False is set globally (app.py:35), unlike line 10 which uses | e. course.title is attacker-controlled, set during course creation (views.py:89 Course.create from POST data['title']) and persisted to the DB, then displayed by the review view (views.py:111 review -> review.jinja2). This is a reachable stored XSS sink not covered by existing GT entries.

NOT VULNERABLE. Uses parameterized query with %s placeholder: cur.execute('...WHERE username = %s', (username,)). The %s is a psycopg2/aiopg parameter placeholder (not Python string formatting). The username value is passed as a separate tuple parameter, so the database driver handles proper escaping. This is the safe pattern for parameterized queries.

NOT VULNERABLE. Uses parameterized query with named placeholders: 'VALUES (%(course_id)s, %(review_text)s)'. The params dictionary {'course_id': course_id, 'review_text': review_text} is passed as a separate argument to cur.execute(q, params). The %(name)s syntax here is a psycopg2 named parameter placeholder, NOT Python string formatting — the key difference from the vulnerable Student.create which uses Python's % operator before passing to execute.

NOT VULNERABLE. Uses parameterized query with named placeholders: 'VALUES (%(title)s, %(description)s)'. The parameters are passed as a separate dictionary to cur.execute(q, {'title': title, 'description': description}). The %(name)s syntax is a psycopg2 named parameter placeholder passed separately to execute(), unlike the vulnerable Student.create which applies Python string formatting (% operator) before calling execute().

NOT VULNERABLE. The expression {{ student.name | e }} uses the Jinja2 escape filter (| e) to explicitly HTML-encode the student name before rendering. Despite autoescape=False being set globally, the explicit | e filter ensures that any HTML special characters in the student name are properly escaped. This stands in contrast to the same template's lines 19-20 which render course data without the escape filter.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of user-supplied registration code directly into a raw SQL query: text(f"SELECT id, code FROM ... WHERE code = '{code}'"). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL through the registration_code form field to bypass registration, extract data, or modify the database.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of user-supplied search parameter into a raw SQL text() fragment: text(f"text like '%{search_param}%'"). The search_param comes directly from request.args.get('search') with no sanitization.

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) via render_template_string() with user-controlled input. The request.path is interpolated into an f-string that is passed to render_template_string(), allowing an attacker to inject Jinja2 template syntax (e.g., {{7*7}}, {{config}}) via a crafted URL path that triggers a 404.

Remote code execution via insecure deserialization. The 'preferences' cookie is base64-decoded and passed directly to pickle.loads() (imported as 'loads' from pickle). An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload, base64-encode it, and set it as the preferences cookie to achieve arbitrary code execution on every request.

Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via urlopen(url) where url is user-supplied from the profile image URL form. An attacker can provide internal URLs (e.g., file:///etc/passwd, http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/) to access internal network resources, cloud metadata endpoints, or read local files.

Stored XSS via the Jinja2 '| safe' filter on note text: {{ note.text | safe }}. Note text is submitted through a CKEditor rich text field, but CKEditor is a client-side control that can be bypassed. An attacker can submit arbitrary HTML/JavaScript as note text, which will be rendered unescaped for all users viewing the home page.

Stored XSS via render_table with safe_columns=['text']. The Bootstrap-Flask render_table macro renders the 'text' column as safe (unescaped) HTML. Note text containing malicious scripts will be rendered without escaping in search results.

Stored XSS via render_table with safe_columns=['text']. The Bootstrap-Flask render_table macro renders the 'text' column as safe (unescaped) HTML. Note text containing malicious scripts will be rendered without escaping on the personal notes page.

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) on the /accounts/<user_id>/notes endpoint. Any authenticated user can view any other user's notes (including private ones) by changing the user_id parameter in the URL. No authorization check verifies that the requesting user owns the requested notes.

IDOR on note deletion. The /notes/<note_id>/delete endpoint does not verify that the authenticated user owns the note being deleted. While the template only renders the delete button for the note owner or admin, the backend has no ownership check — any authenticated user can delete any note by directly sending a POST request with any note_id.

Privilege escalation via mass assignment. The update_account function uses current_user.__dict__.update(filtered_values) to apply all form fields to the user object. The AccountForm includes an is_admin BooleanField, so any user can submit is_admin=y to escalate to admin privileges. The admin checkbox is only hidden client-side (template), not validated server-side.

Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.secret_key = 'super secret key'. This key is used to sign session cookies. An attacker who knows this key can forge session cookies, impersonate any user, and bypass authentication entirely.

Missing @login_required decorator on the POST /account endpoint (update_account function). While the GET /account route requires authentication, the POST route that modifies user account data does not. An unauthenticated attacker could potentially modify account details.

Hardcoded default credentials for seeded users: user@evfa.com/user and admin@evfa.com/admin. These weak, well-known credentials are created on application startup and provide immediate access to both regular and admin accounts.

Hardcoded static registration code 'a36e990b-0024-4d55-b74a-f8d7528e1764' seeded on every application startup. Anyone who knows this code can register new accounts, bypassing the registration code requirement.

NOT VULNERABLE. Line 55 returns current_user.email only when current_user.is_authenticated, so the address goes to the session owner who already knows it; unauthenticated callers receive '-'. The endpoint takes no parameter identifying another account, so it supports neither cross-user disclosure nor enumeration.

SQLAlchemy engine created with echo=True, which logs all SQL statements including potentially sensitive query parameters (passwords, registration codes, user data) to stdout/stderr. This can expose sensitive data in application logs.

The POST /login endpoint (do_login function) has no rate limiting. No Flask-Limiter, SlowAPI, or any throttling middleware is used anywhere in the application. An attacker can make unlimited brute-force login attempts against user credentials. Per classification guidance, missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints is High severity.

The POST /signup endpoint (do_signup function) has no rate limiting. No throttling middleware exists in the application. An attacker can brute-force registration codes to create unauthorized accounts. The registration code validation (validate_token) is called on each attempt with no restriction on frequency. Per classification guidance, missing rate limiting on registration endpoints is High severity.

Stored XSS via <object> tag rendering user-controlled profile image data URI. The template renders: <object data="{{current_user.profile_image.decode() ...}}">. The profile image is set via get_base64_image_blob() which uses guess_type(url) for MIME type. An attacker providing a URL ending in .html causes the stored data URI to be data:text/html;base64,... — the <object> tag renders this as HTML with JavaScript execution. Base64 content passes through Jinja2 auto-escaping unmodified. Exploitation against other users requires chaining with the missing CSRF protection (GT-016) to set a victim's profile image to a malicious URL.

Stored XSS via <object> tag in the base layout template's navbar. The profile image is rendered as: <object data="{{current_user.profile_image.decode() ...}}">. Same attack vector as account.html — attacker-controlled data URI with text/html MIME type executes JavaScript.
