This is higher impact than account.html because base.html is the layout template rendered on EVERY page, meaning the XSS payload executes on every page load after exploitation. Requires CSRF chain (GT-016) to exploit against other users.

The Flask app does not set SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True. Session cookies will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. The nginx configuration (conf/nginx.conf) only listens on port 80 with no TLS, confirming cookies are sent in cleartext. This is a best-practice hardening issue — classified as Low since it's an informational finding for an open-source development/educational application.

The nginx configuration listens exclusively on port 80 (HTTP) with no TLS/SSL listener. All traffic including credentials, session cookies, and user data is transmitted in cleartext. Classified as Low since this is an infrastructure configuration issue for an open-source educational application, though it does enable network-level interception of authentication traffic.

The 'preferences' cookie is set via response.set_cookie('preferences', b64encode(dumps(preferences)).decode()) without httponly=True. This allows JavaScript to read and modify the cookie. Critically, this cookie is deserialized using pickle.loads() in the before_request handler (line 118), so an XSS attack can modify the preferences cookie to a malicious pickle payload, achieving RCE. The missing HttpOnly flag enables this XSS-to-RCE chain — classified as Medium since it's a valid security concern that amplifies existing XSS vulnerabilities.

The download function reads the entire HTTP response with response.read() without any size limit. An attacker can provide a URL pointing to an extremely large file (or a slow-drip endpoint), causing memory exhaustion or resource starvation on the server. Classified as Low per DoS guidance — this is a generic DoS possibility through a normal endpoint that requires authentication to trigger.

The 'preferences' cookie is set via response.set_cookie() in toggle_darkmode (line 105) and after_request (line 127-128) without httponly=True. JavaScript can read and modify this cookie. Critically, the preferences cookie is deserialized using pickle.loads() in the before_request handler (line 118), so an XSS attack can replace the cookie with a malicious pickle payload to achieve remote code execution. The missing HttpOnly flag enables this XSS-to-RCE attack chain. Classified as Medium since it amplifies existing XSS vulnerabilities into RCE.

The 'preferences' cookie is set without secure=True in both toggle_darkmode (line 105) and after_request (line 127-128). This cookie is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections (nginx only listens on port 80). Since the cookie is deserialized with pickle.loads(), a network attacker performing a MITM attack could modify the cookie in transit to inject a malicious pickle payload, achieving RCE. Classified as Low since it requires network-level attacker positioning, but the impact is amplified by the insecure pickle deserialization.

NOT VULNERABLE. The login query uses SQLAlchemy ORM's filter method with a Python equality operator: session.query(User).filter(User.email == form.email.data). SQLAlchemy ORM automatically parameterizes these queries, preventing SQL injection. The email value is never interpolated into raw SQL.

NOT VULNERABLE. The user existence check uses SQLAlchemy ORM: session.query(session.query(User).where(User.email == form.email.data).exists()).scalar(). The ORM parameterizes the email comparison, preventing SQL injection despite the query involving user input.

NOT VULNERABLE. Passwords are properly hashed using bcrypt with a random salt: hashpw(form.password.data.encode('utf-8'), gensalt()). bcrypt is a strong, adaptive hashing algorithm suitable for password storage. The same secure pattern is used in account updates (routes/account.py:88).

NOT VULNERABLE. The search parameter is rendered in the input value attribute using Jinja2's default auto-escaping: value="{{search}}". Jinja2 automatically escapes HTML special characters (<, >, &, ") in template expressions, preventing attribute injection and reflected XSS in this context.

Source of reflected XSS: request.args.get('name', 'world!') is passed unsanitized to render_template where it is rendered with | safe filter in the template

XSS via cookie or form input: {{ name | safe }} renders the 'name' variable (sourced from request.cookies.get('name') or request.form.get('name')) with escaping disabled. Exploitable via cookie manipulation or form submission.
Source of cookie/form-based XSS: request.cookies.get('name') and request.form.get('name') flow unsanitized into render_template where they are rendered with | safe filter

Stored XSS: {{ message.message | safe }} renders user-submitted feedback/message content with escaping disabled. Messages are stored in the database from user input (send_feedback endpoint or unauthenticated API POST) and displayed on the admin messages page, allowing XSS against admin users.

Stored XSS: {{ message.from_user | safe }} renders the from_user field with escaping disabled. The from_user field can be controlled directly via the unauthenticated API POST endpoint (from_user JSON field), enabling stored XSS against admin users viewing the messages page.

Stored XSS injection point: user-submitted feedback from request.form.get('feedback') is stored in Message model without sanitization. The message content is later rendered with | safe in admin/message.html.

Stored XSS injection point via unauthenticated API: message and from_user from JSON request body are stored in Message model without sanitization or authentication. Both fields are rendered with | safe in admin/message.html.

XSS via username: {{ g.user.username | safe }} renders the logged-in user's username with escaping disabled in the navbar. If a user can register with a username containing script tags, it will execute on every page. Exploitability depends on whether user registration exists (not in current code, but flask_admin ModelView for User may allow user creation by admin).

Hardcoded Flask SECRET_KEY: 'Keep it secret, keep it safe'. This secret is used for signing session cookies. An attacker who knows this value can forge arbitrary session cookies, impersonate any user, and escalate privileges.

DEBUG mode enabled in production code: app.config['DEBUG'] = True exposes the Werkzeug interactive debugger, which allows arbitrary code execution if the debugger PIN is known or guessable, and leaks stack traces, source code, and local variables to any user who triggers an error.

Plaintext password storage: User model stores passwords without any hashing. Passwords are stored as plain strings in the database (line 11: db.Column(db.String(200)), line 16: self.password = password). Anyone with database access can read all user passwords.

Password exposed in API serialization: User.serialize property includes the plaintext password field (line 27: 'password': self.password). This is used in the /api/v1/users/ endpoint, exposing all user passwords to anyone with API access. Upstream sites of the same plaintext-storage flow: column declaration at line 11 (`password = db.Column(...)` with no hashing) and `__init__` at line 16 (`self.password = password`).

API endpoint exposes all user passwords: UsersView.index() serializes all users including plaintext passwords via user.serialize. While admin_required decorator restricts access, the admin password itself is 'admin', making this easily exploitable.
Default admin password hardcoded as 'admin' (line 14: password='admin'). The admin user is created with trivially guessable credentials. The login page even displays 'admin/admin' as the credentials.

Open redirect: request.args.get('next') is passed directly to redirect() without any validation. An attacker can craft a URL like /toggle_xss_protection/?next=https://evil.com to redirect users to a malicious site.

Missing authentication on message creation API: MessagesView.post() has no @login_required or @admin_required decorator, allowing any unauthenticated user to submit messages. Combined with stored XSS in the admin message view, this allows unauthenticated attackers to inject XSS payloads targeting admin users.

NOT VULNERABLE by current guidance. The after_request handler sets X-XSS-Protection to 0, disabling the deprecated browser XSS auditor. Current OWASP guidance recommends exactly this value and relies on CSP and output encoding instead.

Plaintext password comparison in authentication: user.password == password compares the submitted password directly against the stored plaintext password. No hashing algorithm is used, meaning passwords are stored and compared in cleartext.
New password stored in plaintext: the change_password endpoint stores the new password directly without hashing: User.query.filter_by(id=current_user.id).update({'password': new_password})

Plaintext password comparison in change_password handler: the current password is compared directly against the stored plaintext password (current_user.password == current_password) at line 26. This is distinct from flask-xss-020 (which covers the new password storage at lines 34-35) and flask-xss-019 (which covers login comparison at login/views.py:17). This is the current-password verification step in the change_password flow, confirming no hashing is used at any point.

Session fixation: login_user(user) is called without regenerating the session ID. Flask-Login does not automatically regenerate session IDs on login without explicit configuration. An attacker who can pre-set a session ID (e.g., via one of the existing XSS vulnerabilities or network access) can hijack the authenticated session after the victim logs in. The attack chain is realistic given the multiple XSS vulnerabilities already present in this application.

Missing rate limiting on login endpoint: no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism exists. Combined with plaintext password comparison (flask-xss-019) and a hardcoded default admin password of 'admin' (flask-xss-015), an attacker can perform unlimited brute-force login attempts with no throttling. This is especially dangerous given the trivially guessable default credentials.

CORRECTED (hand-audited): UsersView is defined in api/views.py but never registered via UsersView.register(api) -- the module's only FlaskView.register() call is MessagesView.register(api), and blueprints/api/__init__.py is empty. The get() handler at line 77 is dead code, unreachable via any route. Original claim: IDOR via sequential integer IDs in UsersView.get().

Admin panel access control based on username string comparison: AdminOnlyMixin.is_accessible() delegates to is_admin_user(current_user), which checks if username equals 'admin'. This is a weak access control pattern — if any user can register or change their username to 'admin', they gain full admin panel access. This is the view-layer enforcement of the weak admin check defined in models.py (see flask-xss-028).

CORRECTED (hand-audited): same UsersView.get() dead-code issue as flask-xss-024 -- UsersView is never registered with the api blueprint, so the sensitive-data-exposure at line 84 is unreachable. Original claim: UsersView.get() exposes full user object including plaintext password.

Full User object with plaintext password passed to every template context via g.user: the before_request handler assigns g.user = current_user, making the complete User model (including the plaintext password field) accessible in every template rendering context. While current templates don't directly render g.user.password, the data crosses a trust boundary into the template layer. This is the root injection point — distinct from flask-xss-009 (template rendering of username) and flask-xss-012/013 (model/API serialization).

Admin role determined by username string comparison: the is_admin property checks if username equals 'admin' rather than using a dedicated role or boolean field. If a user can register with the username 'admin' (or change their username to it), they gain admin privileges. No proper role-based access control exists. This is the model-layer definition that backs the admin panel access control in admin/views.py (see flask-xss-025).

An attacker can bypass authentication or extract data with payloads like ' OR '1'='1' --.

Search Results for {query}

". No output encoding or escaping is applied. An attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript via the q parameter.

". An attacker who sets a malicious cookie value (or exploits the login to set it) can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript. The response also contains a hardcoded demonstrating the issue.

Hardcoded admin credentials at module level: USERNAME = 'admin' and PASSWORD = 'password123'. These credentials are embedded directly in source code, exposing them to anyone with access to the codebase.

Plaintext password storage. User credentials are inserted into the database without any hashing: INSERT INTO users (username, password) VALUES ('user1', 'password1'). The password column stores raw plaintext, allowing full credential compromise if the database is accessed.

The /dashboard endpoint has no authentication check. It reads a 'session' cookie but does not verify it against any session store or validate the user is authenticated. Any user can access the dashboard by navigating directly to /dashboard, defaulting to 'guest' if no cookie is set. There is no server-side session validation whatsoever.

Insecure session management via plain cookie. The session cookie is set with response.set_cookie('session', username) with no HttpOnly flag, no Secure flag, no SameSite attribute, and the value is the raw username (not a signed/encrypted session token). This allows cookie theft via XSS, session spoofing by setting arbitrary cookie values, and transmission over unencrypted connections.

The login form submits via POST to /login with no CSRF token. The Flask app does not use any CSRF protection middleware (e.g., Flask-WTF CSRFProtect). An attacker can craft a page that auto-submits the login form to perform login CSRF attacks.

The /login endpoint accepts POST requests with username/password without any rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection mechanism. The application uses weak hardcoded passwords ('password123', 'password1') and has no throttling on failed attempts. An attacker can perform unlimited credential guessing attempts. No Flask-Limiter or equivalent middleware is configured anywhere in the application.

The init_db function executes SQL statements with hardcoded string literals (CREATE TABLE and INSERT INTO with fixed values). No user input flows into these queries. Although the queries use string literals rather than parameterized queries, there is no injection vector because the values are compile-time constants, not user-controlled data.

The login failure response returns a static HTML string: 'Invalid credentials. Try again'. Although this is raw HTML returned from the endpoint, it contains no user-controlled input — the message is a hardcoded string literal. No XSS is possible because no user data is reflected in this response.

User-supplied 'ip' parameter from request.args is passed directly as an argument to subprocess.check_output(['ping', '-c', '4', ip]) without any validation or sanitization. While the list form prevents shell metacharacter injection, unsanitized input to a system command enables argument injection (e.g., passing flags like '-c 10000') and DNS-based attacks via attacker-controlled hostnames. Most SAST scanners will flag this as command injection.

Username ('admin') and password ('password123') are hardcoded as module-level constants USERNAME and PASSWORD, then used directly in the /login authentication check. Any attacker with source code access obtains valid credentials.

Untrusted data from request.data is passed directly to pickle.loads() at line 33. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload to achieve arbitrary code execution on the server. The /unserialize endpoint accepts raw POST body and deserializes it without any validation.

User-supplied 'id' parameter from request.args is concatenated directly into a SQL query string: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = '" + user_id + "'". This allows classic SQL injection. The query is then passed to run_query() which simulates database execution.

Flask application is run with debug=True (app.run(debug=True)). This enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger which exposes a Python REPL in the browser on unhandled exceptions, allowing arbitrary code execution. It also leaks detailed stack traces, source code, and environment variables to any user.

The /login endpoint at lines 19-26 accepts POST authentication requests with no rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection. This is distinct from the hardcoded credentials finding (CWE-798 at lines 16-17) as it enables network-based brute-force attacks independently of source code access. An attacker can send unlimited authentication attempts with no throttle, lockout, or delay applied at any point in the request handling.

Reflected XSS in the get_user function. The user-supplied 'id' parameter from request.args is concatenated into a SQL query string, passed to run_query() which returns 'Query result for: ' + query (embedding the unsanitized user input), and the result is returned via 'return str(result)'. Flask serves this with text/html content type by default, so an attacker can inject HTML/JavaScript via the id parameter (e.g., id=<script>alert(1)</script>) which will be rendered in the victim's browser. This is distinct from the SQL injection vulnerability (GT-004) at line 46 — both share the same unsanitized input but target different sinks (browser HTML rendering vs database query).

The requests.get() call uses a hardcoded URL ('https://example.com'), not user-controlled input. There is no SSRF vulnerability because the target URL cannot be influenced by an attacker. Scanners may flag the use of requests.get() but the destination is a static constant.

The run_query() function looks like it executes a SQL query but is actually a simulation that only performs string concatenation and returns the result as text. No actual database connection or query execution occurs — it simply returns 'Query result for: ' + query. The real SQL injection vulnerability is at line 46 where the query string is constructed with unsanitized input.

Path traversal via unsanitized 'p' GET parameter joined directly into file path: open(os.path.join(base_path, filename), 'rb').read(). An attacker can use '../../' sequences to read arbitrary files (e.g., ?p=../../settings.py to read Django settings including SECRET_KEY).

Arbitrary code execution via exec() on user-supplied base64-decoded POST data (Python 2 fallback path): exec(base64.decodestring(first_name)). Same vulnerability as the Python 3 path but for Python 2 compatibility.

Unrestricted file upload with no validation on file type, extension, size, or content. The upload endpoint accepts any file and saves it directly using the user-provided filename. An attacker could upload executable files, web shells, or malicious content.

Path traversal in file upload. The original filename from the upload is used directly without sanitization: filename = file.filename, then filepath = os.path.join(UPLOAD_FOLDER, filename). A crafted filename like '../../evil.py' would write the file outside the intended upload directory, potentially overwriting application files.

SSRF in the update_picture API endpoint. The server fetches a user-supplied URL via requests.get(picture_url) with no validation or restriction on the URL scheme, host, or port. An attacker can make the server send requests to internal services (e.g., http://169.254.169.254/ for cloud metadata, internal APIs, or localhost services).

No brute-force protection on the login endpoint. The /login route accepts unlimited authentication attempts with no rate limiting, account lockout, CAPTCHA, or delay mechanism. An attacker can perform credential stuffing or brute-force attacks against user accounts.

JWT tokens are signed with the hardcoded weak secret 'just_another_secret' from Config.SECRET_KEY. An attacker who knows this secret can forge valid JWT tokens to impersonate any user on the API, bypassing authentication entirely.

Missing authentication on profile pictures endpoint. The /uploads/profile_pictures/<filename> route serves profile pictures to anyone without requiring login. An attacker can enumerate and access all user profile pictures by iterating over numeric IDs (1.png, 2.png, etc.).

Error message printed to console on signup failure: print('Error inserting user:', e). In debug mode (which is enabled), this could expose database error details including table structure and SQL errors to the console/logs.

Exception details returned to user in SSRF endpoint error handling: return {'message': str(e)}, 500. This leaks internal error messages, stack traces, and potentially internal network information (hostname resolution errors, connection refused on internal ports, etc.) to the attacker.

Database seeding script hardcodes credentials for user 'bob_brown' with password 'my-secret' and 'write' permissions. This is distinct from the hardcoded SECRET_KEY (threatbyte-005) and JWT secret (threatbyte-017) — those are application secrets, while this is a seeded user account with a known weak password. If the seed data is loaded in any deployed environment, an attacker with source code knowledge can authenticate as bob_brown with write-level access.

The API login endpoint POST /api/v1/login has no rate limiting, account lockout, or brute-force protection. This is a separate attack surface from the web login at /login (covered by threatbyte-016 in server/routes.py). Protecting the web login route does not protect the API login route — they are independent Flask route handlers in separate files. An attacker can perform unlimited credential brute-force attempts against the API endpoint.

The CI workflow downloads the OpenGrep binary via curl from a GitHub release URL (https://github.com/opengrep/opengrep/releases/download/v1.3.0/opengrep_manylinux_x86) without any checksum or signature verification. The downloaded binary is then executed with full access to the repository contents and CI secrets. If the opengrep release is compromised (via supply chain attack, account takeover, or DNS hijacking), a malicious binary would execute in the CI pipeline.

The ZAP DAST baseline scan is run with the -I flag (line 53: '-a -I'), which forces ZAP to return exit code 0 regardless of security findings. This means the CI pipeline will never fail due to DAST results — XSS, SQL injection, and other dynamic findings are silently ignored, allowing vulnerable code to be merged and deployed without any gate.

Login query uses parameterized query with ? placeholders: cursor.execute(query, (username, username)). Despite user input being passed to the query, it is safely parameterized and not vulnerable to SQL injection.
Signup INSERT query uses parameterized query with ? placeholders: cursor.execute(query, (username, email, country, hashed_password)). User-supplied values are safely parameterized.

Dashboard file listing query (when no search term) uses parameterized query: cursor.execute('SELECT filename FROM files WHERE user_id = ?', (user_id,)). This is the safe code path contrasting with the vulnerable search path on lines 137-138.
API login query uses parameterized query: cursor.execute(query, (username, username)) with query = 'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? OR email = ?'. User input is safely parameterized.

File download via send_from_directory(UPLOAD_FOLDER, filename) is NOT vulnerable to path traversal. Flask's send_from_directory() safely resolves the path and raises a 404 if the resolved path is outside the specified directory, preventing directory traversal attacks.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of unsanitized username path parameter into raw SQL query: user_query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '{username}'" followed by db.session.execute(text(user_query)). Reachable from GET /users/v1/{username} without authentication.

Unauthorized password change (IDOR). When vuln=1, the update_password function uses the username from the URL path parameter to look up the user whose password to change, instead of using the authenticated user from the JWT token (resp['sub']). Any authenticated user can change any other user's password by sending PUT /users/v1/{victim_username}/password.

Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA). When vuln=1, get_by_title queries the book by title only (Book.query.filter_by(book_title=str(book_title)).first()) without verifying the authenticated user is the owner. Any authenticated user can read any book's secret_content by sending GET /books/v1/{book_title}.

Mass assignment vulnerability allowing privilege escalation. When vuln=1, the register_user function checks if 'admin' is present in the user-supplied JSON body and uses it to set the admin flag on the new user. An attacker can register as admin by including '"admin": true' in the POST /users/v1/register request body.

Excessive data exposure through unauthenticated debug endpoint. GET /users/v1/_debug returns all user details including plaintext passwords, email addresses, and admin status for every user via User.get_all_users_debug(). No authentication or authorization is required.

User and password enumeration via differential error messages. When vuln=1, login_user returns 'Password is not correct for the given username.' for valid usernames with wrong passwords (line 103) and 'Username does not exist' for invalid usernames (line 106). This allows attackers to enumerate valid usernames. Additionally, the except jsonschema.exceptions.ValidationError as exc: handler at line 112 returns exc.message directly in the 400 response body, leaking jsonschema-internal validator/path detail to the client.

Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS). When vuln=1, update_email uses a complex regex with nested quantifiers: r"^([0-9a-zA-Z]([-.\.\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z])*@{1}([0-9a-zA-Z][-\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z]\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,9})$". The nested groups ([-.\.\w]*[0-9a-zA-Z])* cause catastrophic backtracking with crafted input, consuming excessive CPU.

JWT authentication bypass via weak/hardcoded signing key. The SECRET_KEY used for signing and verifying JWT tokens is hardcoded as the string 'random' (config.py line 13). An attacker who knows this trivially guessable key can forge valid JWT tokens for any user, including admin accounts, achieving complete authentication bypass.

Flask application runs with debug=True (vuln_app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000, debug=True)). This enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger which exposes detailed stack traces with local variable values on errors and may allow arbitrary code execution if the debugger PIN is compromised.

Lack of resources and rate limiting. All API endpoints are registered (vuln_app.add_api('openapi3.yml')) without any rate-limiting middleware or throttling mechanism. This allows unlimited requests to authentication endpoints (login, register) enabling brute-force attacks, and unlimited requests to all other endpoints enabling denial of service. No Flask-Limiter or equivalent is used.

The populate_db() function, exposed as the /createdb endpoint, drops and recreates all database tables and populates them with default data without any authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated attacker can call this endpoint to wipe the entire database, causing complete data loss and denial of service. Data flow: Unauthenticated HTTP request → /createdb route → populate_db() → SQLAlchemy db.drop_all() + db.create_all() + seeded inserts. No auth check at any point in the chain.

The init_db_users() function creates users with hardcoded, trivially guessable credentials: name1/pass1, name2/pass2, and admin/pass1. These default credentials are publicly visible in the source code and will be present after any database reset via /createdb. Any attacker can log in as any user, including the admin account, using these publicly known default credentials. Distinct from vampi-008 which covers the hardcoded JWT SECRET_KEY in config.py — this finding covers hardcoded user account passwords.

The get_all_users() function at lines 19-21 implements a GET /users/v1/ endpoint that returns all registered usernames and email addresses with no authentication check. Any unauthenticated attacker can enumerate all user accounts and email addresses in a single request, enabling targeted phishing and credential stuffing. Distinct from vampi-005 (the /users/v1/_debug endpoint at lines 24-26 which also exposes plaintext passwords) — this is a different function exposing a subset of user data through the regular user listing endpoint.

Plaintext password storage. The User model declares `password = db.Column(db.String(128))` with no hashing applied at write time — `User.__init__` stores the raw value via `self.password = password`, `register_user` instantiates User(password=password, ...) directly from the request body, and `login_user` later compares request_data.get('password') == user.password confirming the column persists cleartext. The plaintext value reaches HTTP via json_debug() and the /users/v1/_debug endpoint (vampi-005). Distinct from vampi-005 (response-sink) and vampi-012 (hardcoded default credentials).

NOT VULNERABLE. error_message_helper (api_views/users.py:12-16) only embeds the passed string in a JSON envelope, adding no stack trace or internal path. The message is exc.message from jsonschema.validate against register_user_schema, which reports which submitted field failed the API's own published contract.

Safe parameterized ORM query. User.query.filter_by(username=request_data.get('username')).first() uses SQLAlchemy ORM's filter_by which automatically parameterizes the query, preventing SQL injection. The username from user input is safely bound as a parameter.

Safe parameterized ORM query. User.query.filter_by(username=request_data.get('username')).first() uses SQLAlchemy ORM's filter_by which automatically parameterizes the query, preventing SQL injection. User-supplied username from the login JSON body is safely bound.

Safe book retrieval with proper authorization (non-vulnerable path). When vuln=0, get_by_title first resolves the authenticated user from the JWT token, then queries Book.query.filter_by(user=user, book_title=str(book_title)).first(), ensuring only the book owner can access the book's secret content.

Safe email regex (non-vulnerable path). When vuln=0, update_email uses the simpler regex '^[a-z0-9]+[\._]?[a-z0-9]+[@]\w+[.]\w{2,3}$' which does not contain nested quantifiers and is not vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking/ReDoS.
SQL injection via f-string interpolation of username query parameter directly into SQL query: f'SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = "{username}";'. No sanitization or parameterization.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of all user-supplied fields (name, username, password, address, email, contact) into an INSERT SQL query. All fields from the User model body are directly embedded in the query string without parameterization.
SQL injection via f-string interpolation of username query parameter into DELETE SQL query: f'DELETE FROM users WHERE username = "{username}";'. No sanitization or parameterization.

SQL injection via f-string interpolation of user.address into DELETE SQL query without even surrounding quotes: f'DELETE FROM users WHERE address = {user.address};'. The lack of quotes makes exploitation even more trivial than the other SQL injections.

NoSQL injection via raw JSON request body passed directly as a MontyDB/MongoDB query. An attacker can send operator-based queries like {"username": {"$ne": ""}} to dump all users, or use $where/$regex operators for data exfiltration. The request.json() output is passed directly to get_nosql_users() with no validation or sanitization of query operators.

When a SQL query returns multiple users, run_sql_query returns raw tuples containing all columns including password hashes at index 3: return {'users': _data}. Single-user responses (lines 155-160) correctly skip the password field, but the multi-user path at line 162 leaks MD5 password hashes. This is reachable via the GET /select endpoint.

Passwords are hashed using MD5 which is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password storage: md5(user.password.encode()).hexdigest(). MD5 is fast to compute making it vulnerable to brute-force and rainbow table attacks. Should use bcrypt, scrypt, or argon2.
The POST /reset endpoint deletes and reinitializes the entire database with no authentication or authorization. Any unauthenticated user can wipe all data by issuing a POST request to /reset.
The DELETE /user endpoint allows any unauthenticated user to delete arbitrary users from both SQL and NoSQL databases. No authentication, authorization, or ownership checks are performed.

NOT VULNERABLE. The GET /find endpoint constructs the NoSQL query with a hardcoded key: get_nosql_users({'username': username}). The username string from the query parameter is used only as a value, not as an operator key. Unlike the POST /find endpoint, an attacker cannot inject MongoDB operators because the query structure is fixed server-side.

NOT VULNERABLE. The init_sql_db function uses f-string interpolation for SQL INSERT queries (lines 102-119), which looks like SQL injection. However, the data comes exclusively from the Faker library (fake.name(), fake.user_name(), etc.), not from user input. No external attacker can control the values inserted into these queries.

Server-Side Template Injection in 404 error handler. request.url is interpolated into a template string via Python % formatting (line 112), then rendered with render_template_string (line 114). Additionally, dangerous builtins dir, help, and locals are passed as template context, facilitating exploitation to achieve RCE.

SQL injection in /search endpoint. User-supplied 'search' parameter from JSON body is interpolated into a raw SQL query via Python % string formatting on line 261: "SELECT ... WHERE username = '%s'" % search_term. The query is then executed directly via db.engine.execute() on line 265. No parameterization or sanitization.

Server-Side Template Injection in the error handler of /search endpoint. When the SQL query raises an exception (e.g., from a malformed SQL injection attempt), the exception message str(e) is interpolated into a template string via % formatting (line 280) and rendered with render_template_string (line 281). Dangerous builtins dir, help, locals are passed as context. An attacker can trigger this by causing a SQL error and injecting Jinja2 template syntax in the search parameter.

Insecure YAML deserialization via yaml.load() without a safe Loader on user-uploaded YAML file. PyYAML 3.12's yaml.load() defaults to the full Loader which can instantiate arbitrary Python objects, enabling remote code execution. An attacker can upload a YAML file containing !!python/object/apply:os.system directives.

JWT signature verification is completely disabled. jwt.decode(token, verify=False) accepts any token regardless of signature validity. This function is used to protect the /get/<cust_id> endpoint (line 227), meaning an attacker can forge arbitrary JWT tokens to bypass authentication and access any customer record.

Hardcoded weak JWT HMAC signing secret: SECRET_KEY_HMAC = 'secret'. This secret is used to sign and verify JWT tokens (lines 86, 184). Since the value is trivially guessable ('secret'), an attacker can forge valid JWT tokens to authenticate as any user.

Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.secret_key = 'F12Zr47j\3yX R~X@H!jmM]Lwf/,?KT'. This key is used for Flask session cookie signing. A known secret key allows attackers to forge session cookies and potentially escalate privileges.

Hardcoded default admin credentials: username='admin', password='admin123'. These credentials are seeded into the database on first request and provide full application access. The password is stored in plaintext (no hashing).

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) in /fetch/customer. Any authenticated user can fetch any customer's record (including credit card numbers) by supplying an arbitrary customer ID. There is no authorization check to verify the requesting user is allowed to access the specified customer record.

Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) in /get/<cust_id>. Any user with a JWT token (even an unsigned/forged one, since insecure_verify is used) can access any customer's record including credit card numbers by changing the cust_id parameter. No ownership or role-based access control.

Credit card numbers (CCN) are exposed in the /fetch/customer API response. The customer_dict includes 'cc_num': customer_record.ccn, returning full credit card numbers in plaintext JSON responses without masking or truncation.

Credit card numbers (CCN) are exposed in the /get/<cust_id> API response. The customer_dict includes 'cc_num': customer_record.ccn, returning full credit card numbers in plaintext JSON responses without masking or truncation.

Detailed exception messages including SQL error details are rendered directly in HTML responses to the user in the /search error handler. str(e) is interpolated into the template on line 280, potentially revealing database schema, table names, and query structure to attackers.

User passwords are hashed using MD5 (hashlib.md5(password).hexdigest()) which is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password storage. MD5 is fast to compute, has known collision attacks, and is trivially brute-forceable with rainbow tables. A proper password hashing algorithm like bcrypt/scrypt/argon2 should be used.

Admin password 'admin123' is stored in plaintext in the database (user.password = 'admin123' on line 63). No hashing is applied before storage, unlike the /register/user endpoint which at least uses MD5. This allows anyone with database access to read the admin password directly.

XXE vulnerability via docx file upload on /xxe_uploader endpoint. User-uploaded .docx files are parsed with python-docx's Document() (line 303). DOCX files are ZIP archives containing XML. With python-docx 0.8.5 and lxml 4.2.1, maliciously crafted OOXML documents with external entity references can be processed. The endpoint is explicitly named 'xxe' indicating intentional vulnerability. An attacker can craft a docx with embedded XXE payloads to read local files or perform SSRF.

Hardcoded secondary HMAC secret: SECRET_KEY_HMAC_2 = 'am0r3C0mpl3xK3y'. While not directly used in the current code, it is a hardcoded secret in configuration that could be used in future JWT or cryptographic operations. Its presence in source code is a security concern.

The /login endpoint (lines 170-194) has no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism. Any attacker can make unlimited brute-force login attempts. This is amplified by the application's use of MD5 password hashing (GT-014) and a known hardcoded admin password 'admin123' (GT-008), making credential discovery via brute force highly practical. The login function simply queries User.query.filter_by() with no attempt throttling.

The /register/user endpoint returns raw exception messages directly in the JSON response on line 167: jsonify({'Error': str(e.message)}). When database operations fail (e.g., duplicate username constraint violations), internal error details including database schema, table names, and constraint names are exposed to the user. This is a distinct instance from GT-013 which covers the same pattern in the /search endpoint at lines 271-281.

NOT VULNERABLE. random.randint(1, 100) is used solely as a prefix on secure_filename(f.filename) (app.py:319-321). The uploader controls the rest of the name and already knows it, and no authentication, authorization or integrity decision depends on the value, so the weak PRNG protects nothing.

The /register/user endpoint returns raw exception messages directly in the JSON response on line 148: jsonify({'Error': str(e.message)}), 404. Internal database error details, schema names, and constraint information are exposed to the client. Distinct from vulnerable-flask-app-019 (/register/customer at line 167) and vulnerable-flask-app-013 (/search at lines 271-281) — same mechanic, different route handlers.

NOT VULNERABLE. The login endpoint uses SQLAlchemy ORM filter_by: User.query.filter_by(username=username, password=password).first(). This generates parameterized queries internally, preventing SQL injection. Unlike the /search endpoint which uses raw SQL string formatting, this ORM-based query is safe.

NOT VULNERABLE to SQL injection. Customer.query.get(customer_id) uses SQLAlchemy ORM's primary key lookup which generates a parameterized query. While this endpoint has an IDOR vulnerability (documented separately), it is not susceptible to SQL injection.

NOT VULNERABLE to path traversal. The uploaded filename is sanitized using werkzeug.utils.secure_filename() on line 296, which strips directory separators and dangerous characters. Additionally, a random integer is prepended to the filename (line 297). The file is saved to a fixed directory (cwd + '/Files/'). These measures prevent path traversal in the file save operation.

NOT VULNERABLE. The index.html template uses Jinja2's {{ url[0] }} and {{ url[1] }} syntax which auto-escapes HTML by default. The URL values come from Flask's url_for() function which generates safe internal URLs, not from user input. No XSS risk here.

Arbitrary file read via path traversal. self.path from the HTTP request is concatenated to cwd at line 14 and opened at line 22 via open(path).read(). The regex filter on line 10-11 (r'/\.\.\/\.\./' with re.match) is trivially bypassable — it only matches a very specific literal pattern at the start of the path and fails for encodings, alternate traversal sequences, or simple variations like '/../etc/passwd'.

SQL injection via string concatenation: conn.execute('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = '+post_id). The post_id parameter is concatenated directly into the SQL query. The regex filter on line 67-68 (r'^\d+$' with re.M) is weak because the re.M flag makes ^ and $ match line boundaries, allowing multiline input like '1\nOR 1=1' to pass the filter.

Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = 'qwerty12345'. This weak, predictable secret key allows attackers to forge session cookies and CSRF tokens, potentially leading to session hijacking.
Hardcoded Flask secret key: app.config['SECRET_KEY'] = '55555'. This trivially weak secret key allows attackers to forge session cookies.
SQL injection via string concatenation: cursor.execute("SELECT ... WHERE username = '" + username + '"'). User-supplied username is concatenated directly into the SQL query string.
SQL injection via str.format(): cursor.execute("SELECT ... WHERE username = '{}'".format(username)). User-supplied username is interpolated into SQL via Python's format() method.
SQL injection via %-formatting: cursor.execute("SELECT ... WHERE username = '%s' % username). User-supplied username is interpolated into SQL via Python's % string formatting operator.
SQL injection via f-string: cursor.execute(f"SELECT ... WHERE username = '{username}'"). User-supplied username is interpolated into SQL via Python f-string.

XSS via unescaped output. The username variable (derived from decrypting a user-supplied cookie at line 26) is rendered into HTML without any escaping: bytes('Hello %s' % username, 'utf-8'). An attacker who controls the encrypted cookie value can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript.

Insecure deserialization via pickle. The Username.pickle() call on line 14 deserializes user-controlled cookie data using pickle (as documented in the commented-out code on line 15: pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(cookies.get('username').value))). Pickle deserialization of untrusted data allows arbitrary code execution via crafted __reduce__ methods.

SSRF via urllib.request.urlopen(url). The url parameter comes from request.args.get('url'). The startswith('https://insecurewebapp.com') check on line 14 is trivially bypassable by using URLs like 'https://insecurewebapp.com.attacker.com/' or 'https://insecurewebapp.com@attacker.com/', allowing the server to fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.

Vulnerable to hash length extension attack. Uses SHA256(secret + payment_information) instead of HMAC for signing payment data. The naive secret-prefix construction allows attackers to append additional data and compute a valid signature without knowing the secret, enabling payment amount tampering.

Vulnerable to hash length extension attack. Uses SHA256(secret + payment_information) instead of HMAC for signing payment data. Same vulnerability as length_extension_attack.py — attackers can extend the signed message and forge valid signatures to modify payment amounts.

SSL/TLS hostname verification disabled: context.check_hostname = False. This allows man-in-the-middle attacks by accepting any certificate regardless of the hostname it was issued for, enabling interception of encrypted traffic.

NOT VULNERABLE at this line. Line 27 is a bare except that sends a 500 and returns, disclosing nothing. The padding-oracle concern the reason describes arises from unauthenticated AES-CBC decryption elsewhere in the file and is a different weakness from CWE-200 at this location.

Pickle deserialization exploit PoC demonstrating RCE. The __reduce__ method returns os.system with a reverse shell command, and pickle.dumps() at line 17 serializes this payload. While this is an exploit tool rather than a vulnerable endpoint, it demonstrates the insecure deserialization attack vector using pickle's __reduce__ protocol.

CORRECTED (hand-audited): the pickle.loads call (line 14-15) that would decode the cookie into `username` is commented out. The only code path that sends an HTML response uses the hardcoded literal username='stranger' (line 22), not any cookie-derived value -- there is no reflected value to escape. Original claim, sourced from an automated scanner pass rather than manual review: reflected XSS via unescaped username derived from a deserialized cookie.

Missing authentication on the create() handler (lines 93-109). The handler accepts POST requests to create new blog posts with no authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated user can insert arbitrary content into the database. Note: the scanner incorrectly labeled this as the 'edit()' handler, but lines 93-109 correspond to the create() function. The actual edit() handler starts at line 112 and also lacks authentication.

AES-CBC padding oracle vulnerability in the decrypt() method. The method at lines 15-20 uses AES-CBC mode with unpad() on decrypted data. When padding is invalid, the exception propagates to the bare except at lines 27-29 which returns HTTP 500, while valid padding returns HTTP 200. This error differential creates a classic padding oracle that allows an attacker to decrypt any ciphertext block-by-block without knowing the key, and potentially forge valid ciphertexts. Distinct from GT-015 which covers the error handler side (lines 27-29); this entry covers the vulnerable crypto implementation itself.

Hardcoded secret value at line 7 used as the signing key for payment signatures. Anyone with source code access can recover the secret and forge valid payment signatures, regardless of the hash construction used. Distinct from GT-012 which covers the weak SHA256 hash construction (CWE-328) at lines 17-18; this entry covers the hardcoded secret itself.

Hardcoded secret value at line 5 used as the signing key for payment signatures. Anyone with source code access can recover the secret and forge valid payment signatures. Distinct from GT-013 which covers the weak SHA256 hash construction (CWE-328) at lines 12-13; this entry covers the hardcoded secret itself.

NOT VULNERABLE. The only route in the file, /redirect_for_payment (lines 16-22), generates a fresh token, builds a payment string with a hard-coded amount, signs it and returns a 302. It reads no request data and changes no state, so there is nothing for a cross-site request to trigger. The hash(secret + data) construction is a separate finding.

Safe parameterized query: conn.execute('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = ?', (post_id,)). Uses ? placeholder with tuple parameter binding, which prevents SQL injection. This is the first (safe) version of get_post, before the second (vulnerable) get_db_connection redefinition.
Safe parameterized query: conn.execute('SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id = ?', (post_id,)). This is the safe version of the SQLI app, using proper parameter binding to prevent SQL injection.

Safe parameterized INSERT: conn.execute('INSERT INTO posts (title, content) VALUES (?, ?)', (title, content)). Uses ? placeholders with tuple parameter binding. User-supplied title and content from request.form are safely bound as parameters.

Safe autoescaped output. The template uses {% autoescape true %} (line 3) and renders comments via {{ comment }} (line 35), which applies HTML escaping. Despite being labeled as an 'XSS vulnerable web app' in app.py docstring, the current template code is safe — Jinja2 autoescaping converts <, >, &, and quotes to HTML entities.

Safe parameterized INSERT: db.cursor().execute('INSERT INTO comments (comment) VALUES (?)', (comment,)). The user-supplied comment is safely bound via ? placeholder parameter binding, preventing SQL injection.

SQL injection via string concatenation in login query. User-supplied 'username' and 'password' parameters are concatenated directly into the SQL string: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM Users WHERE User ='" + uname + "' AND Password ='" + pwd + "'"). An attacker can bypass authentication or extract data with payloads like ' OR '1'='1' --.

OS command injection via os.popen(). The 'server' parameter from the POST request is concatenated directly into a shell command: os.popen('ping -c 3 ' + server). An attacker can inject arbitrary commands using shell metacharacters (e.g., '127.0.0.1; cat /etc/passwd').

Path traversal in ContentHandler. The 'file' query parameter is concatenated directly into a file path: io.open('read/' + file_name, 'rb'). An attacker can read arbitrary files by supplying directory traversal sequences (e.g., ?file=../../etc/passwd).

Path traversal in StaticHandler. The path captured from the URL regex r'/static/(.*)' is prepended with 'static/' and joined with the base directory without any sanitization (lines 40-42), then opened at line 46: open(static_file, 'r'). An attacker can request /static/../../etc/passwd to read arbitrary files outside the static directory.

Reflected XSS in SearchHandler. The 'q' query parameter is passed directly to self.render() as 'query' and 'link' variables. In search.html, these are rendered using {% raw query %} (line 70, HTML context) and {% raw link %} (line 71, JavaScript context), which bypasses Tornado's default auto-escaping. Additionally, X-XSS-Protection is explicitly set to '0' (line 88), disabling the browser's built-in XSS filter.

Debug mode is enabled in production settings: 'debug': True. In Tornado, debug mode enables auto-reload, serves detailed stack traces to clients on errors (information disclosure), and disables template caching. This exposes internal application details to attackers.

Multiple hardcoded credentials in create_db() function. User accounts with plaintext passwords are hardcoded in source: admin/admin (line 140), test-user/test@123 (line 141), sagar/lall0l (line 142), alias/ohrealli (line 143), jacky/st40ngp@55 (line 144), sam/tomTOM123 (line 145), maxi/D@ni3lDizaark (line 146), lelol/Leeee@Looo@!$ (line 147). These credentials are exposed in source control.

Passwords are stored in plaintext in the SQLite database. The CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements store raw password strings without any hashing: cur.execute("INSERT INTO Users VALUES(1,'admin','admin')"). An attacker who gains database access (e.g., via SQL injection) obtains all passwords in cleartext.

The web login endpoint at /user/login has no rate limiting, account lockout, or CAPTCHA. An attacker can perform unlimited credential guessing attempts. The endpoint accepts POST with username/password and calls libuser.login() with no throttling mechanism.

The API key generation endpoint at POST /api/key accepts username/password credentials with no rate limiting or lockout. An attacker can perform unlimited brute force attempts against user credentials via this API endpoint.

Authorization bypass via mass assignment in API post creation. Line 57 sets data['username'] from the authenticated API key, but line 62 calls data.update(request.get_json()) which allows the attacker to override the username field with any value. An authenticated user can create posts as any other user by including '"username": "victim"' in the JSON body.

The MFA enable endpoint (POST /mfa/) has no CSRF protection. An attacker can craft a malicious page that submits the MFA enable form with a known OTP secret, binding the attacker's TOTP device to the victim's account. This is distinct from vulpy-013 which covers the MFA disable endpoint.

S/Key OTP generation utility uses Python's non-cryptographic random module: key = str(random.getrandbits(2048)).encode(). The Mersenne Twister PRNG is predictable and unsuitable for generating security tokens. The commented-out secrets.token_bytes() on line 8 shows the developer was aware of this issue.

The good version's API key generation endpoint at POST /api/key has no rate limiting. Same as the bad version - an attacker can perform unlimited brute force attempts against user credentials via JSON schema-validated username/password.

The good version's web login endpoint has no rate limiting, account lockout, or CAPTCHA. Despite using parameterized queries and Scrypt password hashing, the endpoint allows unlimited authentication attempts.

The good version's MFA enable endpoint (POST /mfa/) has no CSRF protection. Same vulnerability as in the bad version - the form accepts OTP without a CSRF token. While the good version adds a Referer check on MFA disable, the enable endpoint remains unprotected.

The good version's session cookie is set without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite flags: response.set_cookie('vulpy_session', fernet.encrypt(...)). While the cookie is Fernet-encrypted (unlike the bad version's base64), the missing flags still allow JavaScript access and potential interception.

S/Key OTP utility uses SHA-1 (ALGORITHM = 'sha1') for its hash chain via hashlib.new(). SHA-1 has known collision vulnerabilities and is deprecated for security use. While S/Key traditionally uses SHA-1 and preimage attacks are harder than collision attacks, modern security guidance recommends SHA-256 or stronger for all cryptographic operations.
Uses parameterized query with ? placeholder: c.execute("SELECT * FROM posts WHERE username = ? ORDER BY date DESC", (username,)). The username parameter is properly bound, preventing SQL injection.

Uses parameterized query with ? placeholders: c.execute("INSERT INTO posts ... VALUES (?, ?, DateTime('now'))", (username, text)). Both username and text parameters are properly bound via parameterized query.

Uses parameterized query: c.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ? and mfa_enabled = 1", (username,)). The username parameter is properly bound via parameterized query, not vulnerable to SQL injection.

Uses parameterized query: c.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?", (username,)). The good version's login function properly uses parameterized queries and Scrypt password hashing instead of string formatting.

Uses parameterized query for password update: c.execute("UPDATE users SET password = ?, salt = ? WHERE username = ?", (...)). The good version properly uses parameterized queries for the password change operation, unlike the bad version.
